passages: Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious.
Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.
Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion .
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism.
It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty.
Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap.
He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models.

extraction.body: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment. This article has been updated with information from an Nvidia employee. sources.title: ‘Bring Back THE Boss’: Nvidia Employees Petition for Jensen Huang’s Return
passages: “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.

An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action.
The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.

Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.
“Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED.
One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit.
Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.
They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back.
Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who wants to talk about what’s happening?

The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another. One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.” The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment. Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email. Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips. It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation. One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED. Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.” Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

sources.title: Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO, source tells CNBC - CNBC
passages: Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.
The board is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss internal matters.
Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets.
Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO.

The resignation came days after Huang admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia.
Over the weekend, the Financial Times reported that Huang had discussed coming back with allies.
Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO.

coreStoryFacts.text: Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious.
Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.
Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion .
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism.
It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty.
Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap.
He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models.
One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development.
Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.
The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment.
As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers.
Where was Nvidia’s security team? Connie Loizos
Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence.
Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications.
Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.
This article has been updated with information from an Nvidia employee.
“If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.

An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action.

So, it's not too surprising that many tech leaders wish to bring him back.

extraction.body: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China. Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models. Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community. Jensen no longer being CEO would be very very bad for the open model cause in the US. Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion . Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source , whatever happens next. Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology. Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development. Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab. Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem. Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China. The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections. That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons. Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes. Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls. Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed. Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy. As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers. More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs. Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority. TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment. This article has been updated with information from an Nvidia employee. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang. “If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another. One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.” The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment. Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips. It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation. One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED. Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.” Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

passages: Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.
The board is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss internal matters.
Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets.
Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO.

The resignation came days after Huang admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia.
Over the weekend, the Financial Times reported that Huang had discussed coming back with allies.
Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO.

extraction.body: Jensen Huang said he would be "honoured" to return as the boss of tech giant Nvidia if the board asked him to, in his first public comments since his shock resignation. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely," Huang said on X, days after reports he had extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy. He said he had an "outpouring" of calls from company employees, investors and others calling for him to return as CEO of Nvidia. But, as the BBC reported on Monday, Nvidia's board is not considering bringing him back to lead the company. The prospect of Huang returning at this point looks unlikely. The company's board is investigating his conduct , which includes an alleged affair with an Nvidia executive. The AI chip giant is set to report its financial results later on Tuesday, during which the company's interim chief executive, Collette Kress, may address the situation with Huang. Beyond the internal Nvidia investigation, Huang's affair with a woman suspected of being an asset for Beijing is set to see the billionaire questioned before multiple committees of US lawmakers in the weeks ahead. The Nvidia founder said he had "made serious mistakes in my personal life". Nonetheless, Huang's statement appeared to show some hope he would be able to move past the major corporate scandal. Huang said people have continued to "reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics". "If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang added. Many technology executives in recent days have praised Huang's role in the artificial intelligence boom. A petition began circulating online over the weekend calling for his reinstatement at the company. Yet, by Monday, many executives were not openly calling for Huang's return. Brad Gerstner, a major tech investor who knows Huang personally and also holds a significant stake in Nvidia, last week wrote an open letter saying that Nvidia could consider Huang's reinstatement. On Monday, Gerstner said during an event hosted by Semafor that his letter had been misunderstood and the investigation into Huang's conduct needed to run its course. While Gerstner questioned the facts around Huang's departure, he added: "I don't know to what degree he misled the board. If I was on a board I would take that very seriously. Let's be clear no one is above the law." Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. Read about our approach to external linking.

sources.title: Trump says he's OK with Jensen Huang returning as Nvidia CEO, sees no national security risk - CNBC
passages: President Donald Trump said he would be open to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returning to the company he resigned from last week amid the fallout from an extramarital relationship he had with an alleged Chinese spy.
"It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns.
Trump is due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.
He also said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China.
A spokesperson for House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., told CNBC "negotiations are still going" about Jensen Huang testifying before a trio of House committees.

Axios reported last week that Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, prompting a Situation Room confrontation between the men.
Both are traveling with Trump on Monday to Asia, as is Rubio.
The Washington Post reported Friday that Rubio had issued a memo to Trump warning the president about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
"He was doing that because you could have — if you didn't delay it, If you didn't do something — you could have a blow-up with China," Trump said.
"We're having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, and I'll make a decision.
Trump also attempted to defuse tension bubbling within his Cabinet between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Lutnick.

"I think he learned a big lesson," Trump said of Huang when asked by reporters on Monday whether he wants to see the company co-founder reinstated as CEO. Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House before departing for a trip to Asia, downplayed national security concerns stemming from the affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based technology company that U.S. officials suspect of having funneled Nvidia's advanced chips to China. "It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns. Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Trump said, of Alice Huang. extraction.body: “I love our country”: Jensen Huang’s apology comes amid escalating Nvidia probes. On Monday, large trucks began circling the streets of Washington, DC, carrying billboards urging Congress to investigate the Trump administration’s ties with Nvidia’s disgraced CEO Jensen Huang. “Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged. “Trump was in bed with Jensen.” TOP is a nonprofit that describes itself as “dedicated to reining in Big Tech.” Currently, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “ horrible idea. ” Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing. Huang used the moment to say that his interests align with the US’s, saying: I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia. Trump may have learned as early as this spring that Huang was potentially the target of Chinese espionage, but the president claimed recently that he didn’t know Huang was potentially exposed to a Chinese spy as he was becoming a prominent part of Trump’s inner circle, CNN reported . If Trump wasn’t adequately briefed, it raises question about whether the White House acted with “sufficient urgency” to address a serious espionage threat, CNN said. But if Trump is deflecting, an even “graver question” will emerge about why Trump didn’t act on information and instead continued to keep Huang close, CNN said. Instead of distancing himself from the Nvidia CEO, Trump invited Huang to sit at the head table during a state dinner with China’s president Xi Jinping, and last month, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, the nation’s highest scientiﬁc honor, for his AI achievements. “Not only has he continued to do nothing, he’s invited that very CEO into the White House and on state visits to China with him,” Sacha Haworth, TOP’s founder and CEO, told Ars. “And the question we all have to ask is ‘why on Earth would he do that?’” What Trump and Nvidia knew—and when—have become central questions for some Republicans, as well as top Democrats who plan to investigate the scandal when they assume control of key committees in Congress next year. Andrew Yoon, head of research for a nonprofit called CivAI, which warns the public of dangers from AI, told Ars that Huang doesn’t need to be compromised by China to have endangered the US. Prioritizing boosting profits over national security alone is “pretty concerning.” “I think the most notable thing here is that Jensen Huang has been at the absolute forefront of lobbying to be able to sell chips to China,” Yoon said. “He has leveraged his very deep relationships with government, especially President Trump, in order to be able to sell as many Nvidia chips to China as he can get away with. If he could be selling Blackwell chips to China, I’m sure he would be.” Yoon noted that evidence suggests some Chinese AI models have been trained on Blackwell chips. Even with China’s push to prioritize domestic chipmakers like Huawei, Nvidia chips remain “indispensable” to China’s frontier AI goals, Yoon said. And national security experts fear that access to high-end chips will help China advance its military AI or gain economic ground. The White House isn’t commenting on Trump’s relationship with Huang. Among the lawmakers accusing the Trump administration of “corruption” is Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), The Wall Street Journal reported . He has already asked the White House to “preserve all communications” between Trump and Huang. Other lawmakers are “seeking more information about what Trump knew about the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang,” the former Megaspeed CEO whom Huang admitted to having an affair with. They also want to know more about “the administration’s failure to stop artiﬁcial-intelligence chips from going to China,” WSJ reported, and Nvidia’s reportedly $25 million donation to the White House ballroom. “It is not just an intelligence issue; it’s also a potential corruption issue,” Blumenthal said. “There needs to be a really penetrating, comprehensive investigation of all the possible compromises of our intelligence that may have occurred, but also… that Donald Trump is so high on the head of Nvidia, and now is potentially linked to intelligence compromises.” Trump has profited off Nvidia’s success while in office, buying “millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares in his personal brokerage accounts since returning to oﬃce in 2025,” the WSJ reported. The White House maintains that the president has no role in managing his stock portfolio. Other officials advising Trump on AI also benefited from relaxing export curbs, TOP said. On Tuesday, the group issued a report summarizing what the public knows about potential conflicts of interest of two Trump officials: former White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Haworth, TOP’s founder, told Ars she’s concerned that Sacks and Lutnick abused their power to convince Trump to let Nvidia sell cutting-edge technology to China, while standing to “gain astronomical amounts of money.” “The public is outraged by Nvidia’s CEO for compromising our national security, but we didn’t get here because of Jensen Huang’s missteps alone,” Haworth said. If “Nvidia was knowingly doing business with companies tied to illegal chip sales and smuggling with China,” then “the Trump administration was asleep at the wheel,” she said. “White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were protecting their own fortunes rather than looking out for Americans,” Haworth said. If the US fails to hold them accountable for alleged conflicts of interest, “it would send a signal that powerful men once again cannot be held to account and that powerful men are protecting powerful men,” Haworth said. Detailing Sacks’ alleged conflicts, the group cited New York Times reporting that the former AI czar had long supported Huang’s stance that allowing Nvidia to sell more chips in China would help the US stay ahead in the AI race. After Sacks became Trump’s key AI advisor, Huang quickly forged a “tight bond” with him, and “both stood to benefit” from their push to sell chips to China, TOP reported. Also notably, while advising the White House, Sacks opposed policies such as the Trump administration’s recent move to cut off China’s remote access to US-made chips through now-restricted Southeast Asian data centers. Citing Sacks’ alignment with Huang, TOP reported that after just one meeting with the two men, Trump decided to allow Nvidia to sell AI chips to China that the Biden administration had previously blocked. Huang valued his alliance with Sacks, TOP noted, citing reporting that showed Huang declaring last year that Nvidia was “lucky” to have Sacks advising Trump. But TOP is concerned that the alliance was built on mutual financial interest and that Sacks took a part-time role in the Trump administration to avoid divestments or disclosure requirements that might have revealed the extent of his possible conflicts of interest. TOP flagged two areas it believes warrant Congressional investigation. While advising Trump to embrace AI deregulation, Sacks and his firm, Craft Ventures, continued investing substantially in AI. Sacks also stood to benefit from pushing Trump to integrate AI into warfare and national security tools, TOP’s report said. Craft Ventures has invested in Palantir, “a Peter Thiel-founded government contractor seen as a ‘rising star’ in the US Defense Tech World and holding hundreds of millions in US government defense contracts,” TOP said. Even within the Trump administration, officials have turned on Commerce Secretary Lutnick, seemingly looking to blame him for mishandling the Nvidia spying investigation and allowing Trump to maintain close ties with Huang despite apparent intelligence risks. Lutnick has bragged publicly that he promised Huang “really easy access to the President” after joining the administration, TOP reported. That alliance helped push Trump to approve the sale of Nvidia H200s to China, TOP said. And that seemed to directly benefit Lutnick, TOP said, because before he was confirmed as secretary, he was CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, which held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock. “In his role as Secretary, Lutnick is responsible for policing exports of sensitive technology to adversaries and global rivals, like China,” TOP reported. “Lutnick and the company he controls benefited greatly from opening sales of Nvidia chips to China.” Those investments shifted substantially around the same time that Lutnick began facing pressure to “crack down on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips to China,” TOP reported. Cantor Fitzgerald “reduced its Nvidia holdings by nearly 50 percent between September 2025 and March 2026,” TOP said. However, when Trump was reportedly first told of the spying allegations this spring, Cantor Fitzgerald again continued to boost Nvidia. Most prominently, the company helped “finance the expansion of one of Nvidia’s newest business partners, IREN,” facilitating a five-year, $3.4 billion deal between Nvidia and the Australia-based cloud computing provider. Among those now criticizing Lutnick for weak enforcement of export controls that appeared designed to protect Huang’s bottom line is Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. But even with scrutiny coming from within the Trump administration, not everyone is convinced that Lutnick did anything wrong. Yoon suggested that, given Lutnick’s long career, there may be normal explanations for potential financial conflicts. “Maybe a separate question is ‘should people with a long storied history in business and industry be working in government at this level?’” Yoon said. Haworth said the next 48 hours will be critical in determining whether Huang succeeds in returning to Nvidia. “I think it’s going to be incumbent on the incoming Democratic leadership to insist that whether or not he returns, investigations will follow,” Haworth said. Nvidia has also been accused of intervening in a Commerce investigation, which Yoon said could also be “pretty consequential” if any evidence bears that out. “I think it’s pretty unlikely that Huang makes it back to Nvidia any time soon,” Yoon said. “Maybe he goes on a redemption tour and comes back in five years or something, but I’m not really seeing a path forward for him right now.”

On Monday, large trucks began circling the streets of Washington, DC, carrying billboards urging Congress to investigate the Trump administration’s ties with Nvidia’s disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.

“Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged. “Trump was in bed with Jensen.” TOP is a nonprofit that describes itself as “dedicated to reining in Big Tech.”

Currently, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “ horrible idea. ” Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing. Huang used the moment to say that his interests align with the US’s, saying:

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia.

Trump may have learned as early as this spring that Huang was potentially the target of Chinese espionage, but the president claimed recently that he didn’t know Huang was potentially exposed to a Chinese spy as he was becoming a prominent part of Trump’s inner circle, CNN reported .

If Trump wasn’t adequately briefed, it raises question about whether the White House acted with “sufficient urgency” to address a serious espionage threat, CNN said. But if Trump is deflecting, an even “graver question” will emerge about why Trump didn’t act on information and instead continued to keep Huang close, CNN said.

Instead of distancing himself from the Nvidia CEO, Trump invited Huang to sit at the head table during a state dinner with China’s president Xi Jinping, and last month, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, the nation’s highest scientiﬁc honor, for his AI achievements.

“Not only has he continued to do nothing, he’s invited that very CEO into the White House and on state visits to China with him,” Sacha Haworth, TOP’s founder and CEO, told Ars. “And the question we all have to ask is ‘why on Earth would he do that?’”

What Trump and Nvidia knew—and when—have become central questions for some Republicans, as well as top Democrats who plan to investigate the scandal when they assume control of key committees in Congress next year. Andrew Yoon, head of research for a nonprofit called CivAI, which warns the public of dangers from AI, told Ars that Huang doesn’t need to be compromised by China to have endangered the US. Prioritizing boosting profits over national security alone is “pretty concerning.”

“I think the most notable thing here is that Jensen Huang has been at the absolute forefront of lobbying to be able to sell chips to China,” Yoon said. “He has leveraged his very deep relationships with government, especially President Trump, in order to be able to sell as many Nvidia chips to China as he can get away with. If he could be selling Blackwell chips to China, I’m sure he would be.”

Yoon noted that evidence suggests some Chinese AI models have been trained on Blackwell chips. Even with China’s push to prioritize domestic chipmakers like Huawei, Nvidia chips remain “indispensable” to China’s frontier AI goals, Yoon said. And national security experts fear that access to high-end chips will help China advance its military AI or gain economic ground.

The White House isn’t commenting on Trump’s relationship with Huang. Among the lawmakers accusing the Trump administration of “corruption” is Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), The Wall Street Journal reported . He has already asked the White House to “preserve all communications” between Trump and Huang.

Other lawmakers are “seeking more information about what Trump knew about the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang,” the former Megaspeed CEO whom Huang admitted to having an affair with. They also want to know more about “the administration’s failure to stop artiﬁcial-intelligence chips from going to China,” WSJ reported, and Nvidia’s reportedly $25 million donation to the White House ballroom.

“It is not just an intelligence issue; it’s also a potential corruption issue,” Blumenthal said. “There needs to be a really penetrating, comprehensive investigation of all the possible compromises of our intelligence that may have occurred, but also… that Donald Trump is so high on the head of Nvidia, and now is potentially linked to intelligence compromises.”

Trump has profited off Nvidia’s success while in office, buying “millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares in his personal brokerage accounts since returning to oﬃce in 2025,” the WSJ reported. The White House maintains that the president has no role in managing his stock portfolio.

Other officials advising Trump on AI also benefited from relaxing export curbs, TOP said. On Tuesday, the group issued a report summarizing what the public knows about potential conflicts of interest of two Trump officials: former White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Haworth, TOP’s founder, told Ars she’s concerned that Sacks and Lutnick abused their power to convince Trump to let Nvidia sell cutting-edge technology to China, while standing to “gain astronomical amounts of money.”

“The public is outraged by Nvidia’s CEO for compromising our national security, but we didn’t get here because of Jensen Huang’s missteps alone,” Haworth said. If “Nvidia was knowingly doing business with companies tied to illegal chip sales and smuggling with China,” then “the Trump administration was asleep at the wheel,” she said.
“White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were protecting their own fortunes rather than looking out for Americans,” Haworth said.

If the US fails to hold them accountable for alleged conflicts of interest, “it would send a signal that powerful men once again cannot be held to account and that powerful men are protecting powerful men,” Haworth said.

Detailing Sacks’ alleged conflicts, the group cited New York Times reporting that the former AI czar had long supported Huang’s stance that allowing Nvidia to sell more chips in China would help the US stay ahead in the AI race. After Sacks became Trump’s key AI advisor, Huang quickly forged a “tight bond” with him, and “both stood to benefit” from their push to sell chips to China, TOP reported.

Also notably, while advising the White House, Sacks opposed policies such as the Trump administration’s recent move to cut off China’s remote access to US-made chips through now-restricted Southeast Asian data centers. Citing Sacks’ alignment with Huang, TOP reported that after just one meeting with the two men, Trump decided to allow Nvidia to sell AI chips to China that the Biden administration had previously blocked.

Huang valued his alliance with Sacks, TOP noted, citing reporting that showed Huang declaring last year that Nvidia was “lucky” to have Sacks advising Trump. But TOP is concerned that the alliance was built on mutual financial interest and that Sacks took a part-time role in the Trump administration to avoid divestments or disclosure requirements that might have revealed the extent of his possible conflicts of interest.

TOP flagged two areas it believes warrant Congressional investigation. While advising Trump to embrace AI deregulation, Sacks and his firm, Craft Ventures, continued investing substantially in AI. Sacks also stood to benefit from pushing Trump to integrate AI into warfare and national security tools, TOP’s report said. Craft Ventures has invested in Palantir, “a Peter Thiel-founded government contractor seen as a ‘rising star’ in the US Defense Tech World and holding hundreds of millions in US government defense contracts,” TOP said.

Even within the Trump administration, officials have turned on Commerce Secretary Lutnick, seemingly looking to blame him for mishandling the Nvidia spying investigation and allowing Trump to maintain close ties with Huang despite apparent intelligence risks.

Lutnick has bragged publicly that he promised Huang “really easy access to the President” after joining the administration, TOP reported. That alliance helped push Trump to approve the sale of Nvidia H200s to China, TOP said. And that seemed to directly benefit Lutnick, TOP said, because before he was confirmed as secretary, he was CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, which held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock.

“In his role as Secretary, Lutnick is responsible for policing exports of sensitive technology to adversaries and global rivals, like China,” TOP reported. “Lutnick and the company he controls benefited greatly from opening sales of Nvidia chips to China.”

Those investments shifted substantially around the same time that Lutnick began facing pressure to “crack down on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips to China,” TOP reported. Cantor Fitzgerald “reduced its Nvidia holdings by nearly 50 percent between September 2025 and March 2026,” TOP said.

However, when Trump was reportedly first told of the spying allegations this spring, Cantor Fitzgerald again continued to boost Nvidia. Most prominently, the company helped “finance the expansion of one of Nvidia’s newest business partners, IREN,” facilitating a five-year, $3.4 billion deal between Nvidia and the Australia-based cloud computing provider.

Among those now criticizing Lutnick for weak enforcement of export controls that appeared designed to protect Huang’s bottom line is Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. But even with scrutiny coming from within the Trump administration, not everyone is convinced that Lutnick did anything wrong. Yoon suggested that, given Lutnick’s long career, there may be normal explanations for potential financial conflicts.
“Maybe a separate question is ‘should people with a long storied history in business and industry be working in government at this level?’” Yoon said.
Haworth said the next 48 hours will be critical in determining whether Huang succeeds in returning to Nvidia.
“I think it’s going to be incumbent on the incoming Democratic leadership to insist that whether or not he returns, investigations will follow,” Haworth said.
Nvidia has also been accused of intervening in a Commerce investigation, which Yoon said could also be “pretty consequential” if any evidence bears that out.

“I think it’s pretty unlikely that Huang makes it back to Nvidia any time soon,” Yoon said. “Maybe he goes on a redemption tour and comes back in five years or something, but I’m not really seeing a path forward for him right now.”

coreStoryFacts.text: Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang return as CEO, adding, “I threw out the name of Tim Cook, but I would say that Jensen’s reinstatement – I think he learned a big lesson, I guess maybe one lesson more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that.” Trump has suggested Tim Cook step in as Nvidia’s CEO multiple times now.
He has a family situation, which is a rough deal, and what he wants to do is sell chips.” Trump went on to say national security “was not put at risk” by his close relationship with Jensen Huang.
When asked about reports that Alice Huang, one of the women Jensen Huang allegedly had an affair with, was a Chinese spy, the president repeatedly claimed he wasn’t sure if it were true.
“Usually what happens with that is that, any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy,” Trump said.

President Donald Trump said he would be open to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returning to the company he resigned from last week amid the fallout from an extramarital relationship he had with an alleged Chinese spy.
"It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns.
Trump is due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.
He also said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China.
A spokesperson for House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., told CNBC "negotiations are still going" about Jensen Huang testifying before a trio of House committees.

Axios reported last week that Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, prompting a Situation Room confrontation between the men.
Both are traveling with Trump on Monday to Asia, as is Rubio.
The Washington Post reported Friday that Rubio had issued a memo to Trump warning the president about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
"He was doing that because you could have — if you didn't delay it, If you didn't do something — you could have a blow-up with China," Trump said.
"We're having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, and I'll make a decision.
Trump also attempted to defuse tension bubbling within his Cabinet between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Lutnick.
Trump acknowledged on Monday that Lutnick might have delayed putting Megaspeed on the list but defended his rationale as essential for diplomacy.
Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.

Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal erupted, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".
Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
The scandal-hit tech boss was discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times , though Nvidia's board is not considering reappointing him.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump said he would be open to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returning to the company he resigned from last week amid the fallout from an extramarital relationship he had with an alleged Chinese spy. "I think he learned a big lesson," Trump said of Huang when asked by reporters on Monday whether he wants to see the company co-founder reinstated as CEO. Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House before departing for a trip to Asia, downplayed national security concerns stemming from the affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based technology company that U.S. officials suspect of having funneled Nvidia's advanced chips to China. "It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns. Trump is due to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. The president told reporters he is not planning to replace Howard Lutnick as commerce secretary after questions arose about the Cabinet member's handling of export controls involving Nvidia's advanced chips. Republican and Democratic members of Congress have raised concerns about the national security implications of the episode after it was revealed that Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in the 1990s, had an extramarital affair with Chinese businesswoman and alleged spy Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading global supplier of advanced artificial intelligence chips. Critics argue the affair could jeopardize the U.S.' global dominance in AI and that it raises questions about influence exerted by Nvidia's Huang on regulators and lawmakers as he opposed export controls that limited the sale of the company's chips to Chinese firms. The New York Times reported Tuesday that the U.S. believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and that Secretary of State Marco Rubio alerted Trump to the situation aboard Air Force One in May before Jensen Huang joined the president on a flight to China. The Washington Post reported Friday that Rubio had issued a memo to Trump warning the president about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. But Trump on Monday said "I haven't heard that" when asked about Rubio's warning. "I don't know that she is a spy. Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy," Trump said, of Alice Huang. "I don't know that she was a spy at all." Trump also attempted to defuse tension bubbling within his Cabinet between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Lutnick. Axios reported last week that Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, prompting a Situation Room confrontation between the men. Both are traveling with Trump on Monday to Asia, as is Rubio. And Bessent, in an appearance on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday, seemed to express frustration at Lutnick for not putting Megaspeed, Alice Huang's former company, on a Commerce Department list of companies that pose national security concerns. The departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the 'entity list' for months," Bessent said. Trump acknowledged on Monday that Lutnick might have delayed putting Megaspeed on the list but defended his rationale as essential for diplomacy. "He was doing that because you could have — if you didn't delay it, If you didn't do something — you could have a blow-up with China," Trump said. "We're having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, and I'll make a decision. But I understand very well both sides." Trump, who previously had said he did not plan to raise the Jensen Huang issue with Xi when they meet this week, said he may do so. He also said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China. As Trump downplays concerns about fallout from the affair and advanced chips finding their way to China, Capitol Hill leaders are taking a different approach . A spokesperson for House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., told CNBC "negotiations are still going" about Jensen Huang testifying before a trio of House committees. Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford, R-Ark., had given Huang a deadline of 8 p.m. ET Friday to respond to their request to appear before the committees. Mast has said he would subpoena the former CEO if he doesn't accept the invitation voluntarily. Got a confidential news tip? We want to hear from you. extraction.body: “I love our country”: Jensen Huang’s apology comes amid escalating Nvidia probes. On Monday, large trucks began circling the streets of Washington, DC, carrying billboards urging Congress to investigate the Trump administration’s ties with Nvidia’s disgraced CEO Jensen Huang. “Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged. “Trump was in bed with Jensen.” TOP is a nonprofit that describes itself as “dedicated to reining in Big Tech.” Currently, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “ horrible idea. ” Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing. Huang used the moment to say that his interests align with the US’s, saying: I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia. Trump may have learned as early as this spring that Huang was potentially the target of Chinese espionage, but the president claimed recently that he didn’t know Huang was potentially exposed to a Chinese spy as he was becoming a prominent part of Trump’s inner circle, CNN reported . If Trump wasn’t adequately briefed, it raises question about whether the White House acted with “sufficient urgency” to address a serious espionage threat, CNN said. But if Trump is deflecting, an even “graver question” will emerge about why Trump didn’t act on information and instead continued to keep Huang close, CNN said. Instead of distancing himself from the Nvidia CEO, Trump invited Huang to sit at the head table during a state dinner with China’s president Xi Jinping, and last month, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, the nation’s highest scientiﬁc honor, for his AI achievements. “Not only has he continued to do nothing, he’s invited that very CEO into the White House and on state visits to China with him,” Sacha Haworth, TOP’s founder and CEO, told Ars. “And the question we all have to ask is ‘why on Earth would he do that?’” What Trump and Nvidia knew—and when—have become central questions for some Republicans, as well as top Democrats who plan to investigate the scandal when they assume control of key committees in Congress next year. Andrew Yoon, head of research for a nonprofit called CivAI, which warns the public of dangers from AI, told Ars that Huang doesn’t need to be compromised by China to have endangered the US. Prioritizing boosting profits over national security alone is “pretty concerning.” “I think the most notable thing here is that Jensen Huang has been at the absolute forefront of lobbying to be able to sell chips to China,” Yoon said. “He has leveraged his very deep relationships with government, especially President Trump, in order to be able to sell as many Nvidia chips to China as he can get away with. If he could be selling Blackwell chips to China, I’m sure he would be.” Yoon noted that evidence suggests some Chinese AI models have been trained on Blackwell chips. Even with China’s push to prioritize domestic chipmakers like Huawei, Nvidia chips remain “indispensable” to China’s frontier AI goals, Yoon said. And national security experts fear that access to high-end chips will help China advance its military AI or gain economic ground. The White House isn’t commenting on Trump’s relationship with Huang. Among the lawmakers accusing the Trump administration of “corruption” is Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), The Wall Street Journal reported . He has already asked the White House to “preserve all communications” between Trump and Huang. Other lawmakers are “seeking more information about what Trump knew about the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang,” the former Megaspeed CEO whom Huang admitted to having an affair with. They also want to know more about “the administration’s failure to stop artiﬁcial-intelligence chips from going to China,” WSJ reported, and Nvidia’s reportedly $25 million donation to the White House ballroom. “It is not just an intelligence issue; it’s also a potential corruption issue,” Blumenthal said. “There needs to be a really penetrating, comprehensive investigation of all the possible compromises of our intelligence that may have occurred, but also… that Donald Trump is so high on the head of Nvidia, and now is potentially linked to intelligence compromises.” Trump has profited off Nvidia’s success while in office, buying “millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares in his personal brokerage accounts since returning to oﬃce in 2025,” the WSJ reported. The White House maintains that the president has no role in managing his stock portfolio. Other officials advising Trump on AI also benefited from relaxing export curbs, TOP said. On Tuesday, the group issued a report summarizing what the public knows about potential conflicts of interest of two Trump officials: former White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Haworth, TOP’s founder, told Ars she’s concerned that Sacks and Lutnick abused their power to convince Trump to let Nvidia sell cutting-edge technology to China, while standing to “gain astronomical amounts of money.” “The public is outraged by Nvidia’s CEO for compromising our national security, but we didn’t get here because of Jensen Huang’s missteps alone,” Haworth said. If “Nvidia was knowingly doing business with companies tied to illegal chip sales and smuggling with China,” then “the Trump administration was asleep at the wheel,” she said. “White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were protecting their own fortunes rather than looking out for Americans,” Haworth said. If the US fails to hold them accountable for alleged conflicts of interest, “it would send a signal that powerful men once again cannot be held to account and that powerful men are protecting powerful men,” Haworth said. Detailing Sacks’ alleged conflicts, the group cited New York Times reporting that the former AI czar had long supported Huang’s stance that allowing Nvidia to sell more chips in China would help the US stay ahead in the AI race. After Sacks became Trump’s key AI advisor, Huang quickly forged a “tight bond” with him, and “both stood to benefit” from their push to sell chips to China, TOP reported. Also notably, while advising the White House, Sacks opposed policies such as the Trump administration’s recent move to cut off China’s remote access to US-made chips through now-restricted Southeast Asian data centers. Citing Sacks’ alignment with Huang, TOP reported that after just one meeting with the two men, Trump decided to allow Nvidia to sell AI chips to China that the Biden administration had previously blocked. Huang valued his alliance with Sacks, TOP noted, citing reporting that showed Huang declaring last year that Nvidia was “lucky” to have Sacks advising Trump. But TOP is concerned that the alliance was built on mutual financial interest and that Sacks took a part-time role in the Trump administration to avoid divestments or disclosure requirements that might have revealed the extent of his possible conflicts of interest. TOP flagged two areas it believes warrant Congressional investigation. While advising Trump to embrace AI deregulation, Sacks and his firm, Craft Ventures, continued investing substantially in AI. Sacks also stood to benefit from pushing Trump to integrate AI into warfare and national security tools, TOP’s report said. Craft Ventures has invested in Palantir, “a Peter Thiel-founded government contractor seen as a ‘rising star’ in the US Defense Tech World and holding hundreds of millions in US government defense contracts,” TOP said. Even within the Trump administration, officials have turned on Commerce Secretary Lutnick, seemingly looking to blame him for mishandling the Nvidia spying investigation and allowing Trump to maintain close ties with Huang despite apparent intelligence risks. Lutnick has bragged publicly that he promised Huang “really easy access to the President” after joining the administration, TOP reported. That alliance helped push Trump to approve the sale of Nvidia H200s to China, TOP said. And that seemed to directly benefit Lutnick, TOP said, because before he was confirmed as secretary, he was CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, which held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock. “In his role as Secretary, Lutnick is responsible for policing exports of sensitive technology to adversaries and global rivals, like China,” TOP reported. “Lutnick and the company he controls benefited greatly from opening sales of Nvidia chips to China.” Those investments shifted substantially around the same time that Lutnick began facing pressure to “crack down on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips to China,” TOP reported. Cantor Fitzgerald “reduced its Nvidia holdings by nearly 50 percent between September 2025 and March 2026,” TOP said. However, when Trump was reportedly first told of the spying allegations this spring, Cantor Fitzgerald again continued to boost Nvidia. Most prominently, the company helped “finance the expansion of one of Nvidia’s newest business partners, IREN,” facilitating a five-year, $3.4 billion deal between Nvidia and the Australia-based cloud computing provider. Among those now criticizing Lutnick for weak enforcement of export controls that appeared designed to protect Huang’s bottom line is Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. But even with scrutiny coming from within the Trump administration, not everyone is convinced that Lutnick did anything wrong. Yoon suggested that, given Lutnick’s long career, there may be normal explanations for potential financial conflicts. “Maybe a separate question is ‘should people with a long storied history in business and industry be working in government at this level?’” Yoon said. Haworth said the next 48 hours will be critical in determining whether Huang succeeds in returning to Nvidia. “I think it’s going to be incumbent on the incoming Democratic leadership to insist that whether or not he returns, investigations will follow,” Haworth said. Nvidia has also been accused of intervening in a Commerce investigation, which Yoon said could also be “pretty consequential” if any evidence bears that out. “I think it’s pretty unlikely that Huang makes it back to Nvidia any time soon,” Yoon said. “Maybe he goes on a redemption tour and comes back in five years or something, but I’m not really seeing a path forward for him right now.”

“Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged. “Trump was in bed with Jensen.” TOP is a nonprofit that describes itself as “dedicated to reining in Big Tech.”

Currently, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “ horrible idea. ” Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing. Huang used the moment to say that his interests align with the US’s, saying:

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. But if Trump is deflecting, an even “graver question” will emerge about why Trump didn’t act on information and instead continued to keep Huang close, CNN said.

Instead of distancing himself from the Nvidia CEO, Trump invited Huang to sit at the head table during a state dinner with China’s president Xi Jinping, and last month, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, the nation’s highest scientiﬁc honor, for his AI achievements.

“Not only has he continued to do nothing, he’s invited that very CEO into the White House and on state visits to China with him,” Sacha Haworth, TOP’s founder and CEO, told Ars. “And the question we all have to ask is ‘why on Earth would he do that?’”

Andrew Yoon, head of research for a nonprofit called CivAI, which warns the public of dangers from AI, told Ars that Huang doesn’t need to be compromised by China to have endangered the US. If he could be selling Blackwell chips to China, I’m sure he would be.”

Yoon noted that evidence suggests some Chinese AI models have been trained on Blackwell chips. Even with China’s push to prioritize domestic chipmakers like Huawei, Nvidia chips remain “indispensable” to China’s frontier AI goals, Yoon said. And national security experts fear that access to high-end chips will help China advance its military AI or gain economic ground.

The White House isn’t commenting on Trump’s relationship with Huang. Among the lawmakers accusing the Trump administration of “corruption” is Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), The Wall Street Journal reported . He has already asked the White House to “preserve all communications” between Trump and Huang.

Other lawmakers are “seeking more information about what Trump knew about the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang,” the former Megaspeed CEO whom Huang admitted to having an affair with. They also want to know more about “the administration’s failure to stop artiﬁcial-intelligence chips from going to China,” WSJ reported, and Nvidia’s reportedly $25 million donation to the White House ballroom.

“It is not just an intelligence issue; it’s also a potential corruption issue,” Blumenthal said. “There needs to be a really penetrating, comprehensive investigation of all the possible compromises of our intelligence that may have occurred, but also… that Donald Trump is so high on the head of Nvidia, and now is potentially linked to intelligence compromises.”

Trump has profited off Nvidia’s success while in office, buying “millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares in his personal brokerage accounts since returning to oﬃce in 2025,” the WSJ reported. The White House maintains that the president has no role in managing his stock portfolio.

Other officials advising Trump on AI also benefited from relaxing export curbs, TOP said. On Tuesday, the group issued a report summarizing what the public knows about potential conflicts of interest of two Trump officials: former White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Haworth, TOP’s founder, told Ars she’s concerned that Sacks and Lutnick abused their power to convince Trump to let Nvidia sell cutting-edge technology to China, while standing to “gain astronomical amounts of money.”

“The public is outraged by Nvidia’s CEO for compromising our national security, but we didn’t get here because of Jensen Huang’s missteps alone,” Haworth said. If “Nvidia was knowingly doing business with companies tied to illegal chip sales and smuggling with China,” then “the Trump administration was asleep at the wheel,” she said.
“White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were protecting their own fortunes rather than looking out for Americans,” Haworth said.

If the US fails to hold them accountable for alleged conflicts of interest, “it would send a signal that powerful men once again cannot be held to account and that powerful men are protecting powerful men,” Haworth said.

Detailing Sacks’ alleged conflicts, the group cited New York Times reporting that the former AI czar had long supported Huang’s stance that allowing Nvidia to sell more chips in China would help the US stay ahead in the AI race. After Sacks became Trump’s key AI advisor, Huang quickly forged a “tight bond” with him, and “both stood to benefit” from their push to sell chips to China, TOP reported.

Also notably, while advising the White House, Sacks opposed policies such as the Trump administration’s recent move to cut off China’s remote access to US-made chips through now-restricted Southeast Asian data centers. “Maybe a separate question is ‘should people with a long storied history in business and industry be working in government at this level?’” Yoon said.

On behalf of our shareholders, the board is proactively dealing with the immediately the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward.

In a statement posted to X, he wrote that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone” at the company, that he regretted his mistakes, and that he would cooperate with the Nvidia board’s investigation into his actions. He added that he’d be willing to return to the chief executive role if offered it, though a day earlier, the Nvidia board reportedly said it was not considering bringing him back. “NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” Huang wrote. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” But since his November 12th resignation, Huang remains entangled in scandal. He’s reportedly had three affairs, two with subordinates at Nvidia, one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset suspected of facilitating illicit chip sales. (Huang has pushed against restrictions on Nvidia chip sales in China.) He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st, and an internal company investigation is ongoing. Tech industry heavyweights have still voiced their support for Huang, dubbing him “irreplaceable” and petitioning for his return. Some have cast doubt on the allegations that Alice Huang (no relation) was spying on behalf of China and painted the leaks about their relationship as a conspiracy against the former CEO. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Huang for much of the past year, has also backed him. On Monday, Trump said he “would not mind” Huang returning, adding that “I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another.” Trump’s closeness with Huang could also complicate things for Nvidia, however. The company has ramped up its lobbying in Washington, D.C., spending $5 million in 2025 and $4.7 million so far in 2026. But as Democrats prepare to take Congress, they’re planning to investigate Trump’s dealings with Big Tech and other industries, alleging potential corruption. “The election wasn’t very positive for AI, and [the news around Huang’s resignation] is only going to complicate things, especially for the company in particular but for AI as a whole going forward,” Brendan Glavin, director of insights at OpenSecrets, told The Verge in an interview last week. Lior Prosor, managing partner at Deep33, a tech VC firm, said last week that he didn’t expect Huang’s resignation to pop the AI bubble, although Huang has had a significant hand in mobilizing funds for the AI infrastructure buildout in the U.S. Under Huang’s leadership in August, Nvidia entered into partnerships with six financial institutions for about $500 billion to fund such endeavors. “NVIDIA supplies roughly 75 percent of the AI compute hardware the industry consumes, and demand continues to dramatically outpace supply,” Deep33’s Prosor said in an interview with The Verge. “Neither its customers nor its competitors can easily replace the capabilities it provides, and the economic incentives driving the AI trade remain unchanged.” Even so, a potential market cooling has some worried, as Anthropic’s IPO, slated to potentially be the largest of all time, is set for Thursday. The chipmaker had agreed to buy $10 billion in Anthropic shares via private placement, on top of a $10 billion funding promise Nvidia had already made last year.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” But since his November 12th resignation, Huang remains entangled in scandal.

He’s reportedly had three affairs, two with subordinates at Nvidia, one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset suspected of facilitating illicit chip sales. (Huang has pushed against restrictions on Nvidia chip sales in China.) He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st, and an internal company investigation is ongoing.
Tech industry heavyweights have still voiced their support for Huang, dubbing him “irreplaceable” and petitioning for his return.
Some have cast doubt on the allegations that Alice Huang (no relation) was spying on behalf of China and painted the leaks about their relationship as a conspiracy against the former CEO.
President Donald Trump, a close ally of Huang for much of the past year, has also backed him.

The company has ramped up its lobbying in Washington, D.C., spending $5 million in 2025 and $4.7 million so far in 2026.
But as Democrats prepare to take Congress, they’re planning to investigate Trump’s dealings with Big Tech and other industries, alleging potential corruption.
