Lior Prosor, managing partner at Deep33, a tech VC firm, said last week that he didn’t expect Huang’s resignation to pop the AI bubble, although Huang has had a significant hand in mobilizing funds for the AI infrastructure buildout in the U.S.
Under Huang’s leadership in August, Nvidia entered into partnerships with six financial institutions for about $500 billion to fund such endeavors.
“NVIDIA supplies roughly 75 percent of the AI compute hardware the industry consumes, and demand continues to dramatically outpace supply,” Deep33’s Prosor said in an interview with The Verge.

“Neither its customers nor its competitors can easily replace the capabilities it provides, and the economic incentives driving the AI trade remain unchanged.” Even so, a potential market cooling has some worried, as Anthropic’s IPO, slated to potentially be the largest of all time, is set for Thursday.
The chipmaker had agreed to buy $10 billion in Anthropic shares via private placement, on top of a $10 billion funding promise Nvidia had already made last year.

Nvidia ( NVDA ) board Chairman Harvey Jones said on the company's third quarter earnings call that it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, a week after he resigned from the post following "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct." As Chairman of Nvidia's Board of Directors, I want to say a few words on the board's behalf. Nvidia is an exceptionally strong company. Its strength comes from its extraordinary people, groundbreaking technology and exemplary track record of execution. On November 12th, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms, Jensen Wong voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO. The board appointed Colette Press, Nvidia's long-time and well-respected CFO as interim CEO. In addition, the board announced it was initiating a search for a permanent chief executive, and we have since retained Heidrick & Struggles to lead the search. While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interests of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders. This morning, the company announced that our board has established a National Security and Export control oversight Committee that will include a select group of our independent board directors, senior external advisors and legal council. This committee will enhan- will, excuse me, will enhance our engagement with the US government including all relevant agencies. We will not be addressing or taking questions on today's call regarding the circumstances of Jensen's resignation and the ongoing investigation. Our board will communicate further when appropriate. On behalf of our shareholders, the board is proactively dealing with the immediately the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward. We have an incredibly talented leadership team, and we have every confidence in Colette's leadership, integrity, and ability to deliver as interim CEO.

As Chairman of Nvidia's Board of Directors, I want to say a few words on the board's behalf.
Nvidia is an exceptionally strong company. Its strength comes from its extraordinary people, groundbreaking technology and exemplary track record of execution.

On November 12th, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms, Jensen Wong voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO and board member.
The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.
The board appointed Colette Press, Nvidia's long-time and well-respected CFO as interim CEO.
In addition, the board announced it was initiating a search for a permanent chief executive, and we have since retained Heidrick & Struggles to lead the search.
While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interests of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders.

This morning, the company announced that our board has established a National Security and Export control oversight Committee that will include a select group of our independent board directors, senior external advisors and legal council.
This committee will enhan- will, excuse me, will enhance our engagement with the US government including all relevant agencies.
We will not be addressing or taking questions on today's call regarding the circumstances of Jensen's resignation and the ongoing investigation.
Our board will communicate further when appropriate.
On behalf of our shareholders, the board is proactively dealing with the immediately the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward.
We have an incredibly talented leadership team, and we have every confidence in Colette's leadership, integrity, and ability to deliver as interim CEO.

sources.title: Nvidia says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
passages: Starting Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday, new board chair Harvey Jones said that when former CEO Jensen Huang resigned, “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones added, “We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.” Huang had publicly floated the idea of returning earlier on Tuesday.
“NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” Huang wrote.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” But since his November 12th resignation, Huang remains entangled in scandal.

On Monday, Trump said he “would not mind” Huang returning, adding that “I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another.” Trump’s closeness with Huang could also complicate things for Nvidia, however.
Under Huang’s leadership in August, Nvidia entered into partnerships with six financial institutions for about $500 billion to fund such endeavors.

He’s reportedly had three affairs, two with subordinates at Nvidia, one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset suspected of facilitating illicit chip sales. (Huang has pushed against restrictions on Nvidia chip sales in China.) He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st, and an internal company investigation is ongoing.
“NVIDIA supplies roughly 75 percent of the AI compute hardware the industry consumes, and demand continues to dramatically outpace supply,” Deep33’s Prosor said in an interview with The Verge.
The chipmaker had agreed to buy $10 billion in Anthropic shares via private placement, on top of a $10 billion funding promise Nvidia had already made last year.
Some have cast doubt on the allegations that Alice Huang (no relation) was spying on behalf of China and painted the leaks about their relationship as a conspiracy against the former CEO.

extraction.body: Starting Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday, new board chair Harvey Jones said that when former CEO Jensen Huang resigned, “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones added, “We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.” Huang had publicly floated the idea of returning earlier on Tuesday. In a statement posted to X, he wrote that he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone” at the company, that he regretted his mistakes, and that he would cooperate with the Nvidia board’s investigation into his actions. He added that he’d be willing to return to the chief executive role if offered it, though a day earlier, the Nvidia board reportedly said it was not considering bringing him back. “NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” Huang wrote. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” But since his November 12th resignation, Huang remains entangled in scandal. He’s reportedly had three affairs, two with subordinates at Nvidia, one with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset suspected of facilitating illicit chip sales. (Huang has pushed against restrictions on Nvidia chip sales in China.) He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st, and an internal company investigation is ongoing. Tech industry heavyweights have still voiced their support for Huang, dubbing him “irreplaceable” and petitioning for his return. Some have cast doubt on the allegations that Alice Huang (no relation) was spying on behalf of China and painted the leaks about their relationship as a conspiracy against the former CEO. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Huang for much of the past year, has also backed him. On Monday, Trump said he “would not mind” Huang returning, adding that “I think he learned a big lesson — I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another.” Trump’s closeness with Huang could also complicate things for Nvidia, however. The company has ramped up its lobbying in Washington, D.C., spending $5 million in 2025 and $4.7 million so far in 2026. But as Democrats prepare to take Congress, they’re planning to investigate Trump’s dealings with Big Tech and other industries, alleging potential corruption. “The election wasn’t very positive for AI, and [the news around Huang’s resignation] is only going to complicate things, especially for the company in particular but for AI as a whole going forward,” Brendan Glavin, director of insights at OpenSecrets, told The Verge in an interview last week. Lior Prosor, managing partner at Deep33, a tech VC firm, said last week that he didn’t expect Huang’s resignation to pop the AI bubble, although Huang has had a significant hand in mobilizing funds for the AI infrastructure buildout in the U.S. Under Huang’s leadership in August, Nvidia entered into partnerships with six financial institutions for about $500 billion to fund such endeavors. “NVIDIA supplies roughly 75 percent of the AI compute hardware the industry consumes, and demand continues to dramatically outpace supply,” Deep33’s Prosor said in an interview with The Verge. “Neither its customers nor its competitors can easily replace the capabilities it provides, and the economic incentives driving the AI trade remain unchanged.” Even so, a potential market cooling has some worried, as Anthropic’s IPO, slated to potentially be the largest of all time, is set for Thursday. The chipmaker had agreed to buy $10 billion in Anthropic shares via private placement, on top of a $10 billion funding promise Nvidia had already made last year.

extraction.body: This is CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia's third-quarter 2027 earnings. Nvidia beat on profit and revenue after the bell on Tuesday and issued strong guidance, in the chipmaker's first earnings report since co-founder Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation last week as CEO. The stock rose more than 3% in extended trading. Here's how the company did compared to analysts' estimates, according to LSEG: Revenue more than doubled from $57 billion a year earlier, Nvidia said, a sign of continued strength in its core data center business. The company said revenue this quarter will expand by roughly 90% to about $130 billion, topping the $125.1 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. Finance chief Colette Kress is used to addressing Wall Street, but never like this . She's now functioning as interim CEO, meaning her responsibilities go well beyond the key numbers. At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board doesn't intend to bring Huang back as CEO. The biggest cloud for Nvidia is around its China business after Huang's reported affair with a businesswoman who's allegedly a Chinese spy. The Commerce Department on Monday announced a change that would prevent Nvidia's chips from being rented to Chinese companies entirely, putting revenue at risk. Nvidia kept with its recent language on China, telling investors in its commentary, "We are not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in our outlook." One of the central questions from investors heading into the call was whether Nvidia would scrap a previous forecast for 70% growth in the fiscal year ending in January 2028. However, Kress raised guidance, saying that Nvidia now expects 75% growth. Kress said during the Q&A portion of the call that it's "business as usual at Nvidia." "Our leadership has stood up so strongly over the last week to support both what we are doing here at earnings, but also supporting all of our different employees around the world," she said. "Remember, we have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap. And I think that's important from a business perspective." Nvidia's stock is down 24% this month and on Friday wrapped up its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012. The stock has dropped the first two days of this week and is trading at its lowest since July 2025. In addition to the Huang saga, the company is dealing with broader concerns about an AI slowdown and a political shift in Washington, D.C., following this month's midterm elections. Gene Munster, managing partner of Deepwater Asset Management, said investors should focus on Nvidia's business outlook as the board searches for a permanent CEO. "What we need in terms of chips, what we need in terms of advanced packaging or memory, all of that is also coming together," Kress said. "We felt very confident, therefore, that we could establish that we will grow 75% over year over year in terms of fiscal year 28." Kress was brought in as interim CEO last week after 13 years as Nvidia's CFO. She previously served in financial roles at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments. The board is in the process of selecting a long-term CEO, hiring executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to lead the hunt, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said on the earnings call. Jones said the board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Huang said in a statement Tuesday that he's open to returning, and an online petition calling for his reinstatement has nearly 200,000 signatures. Kress said that it is "business as usual" at Nvidia, and that representatives from TSMC had visited Nvidia this week. "It's business as usual. We've engaged with our customers, we've engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They're all 100% behind us," Kress said. Nvidia's commitments to secure supply of parts for its chips and systems increased to $390 million from $279 billion in the prior period. The sharp increase is primarily related to the multi-year procurement of memory supply, the company said in its earnings commentary. Nvidia data center lease commitments and cloud service agreements came to $102 billion, up from $74 billion in the last quarter. Nvidia reported $8.2 billion in third-quarter edge computing revenue, a category that includes robotics- related products as well as its graphics cards for gamers and running AI at home. That topped a StreetAccount estimate of $7.47 billion, and represents 42% annual growth — lower than the company's data center business, but still robust. One of the big concerns in the AI trade has been the health of the neoclouds, which rely on the capital markets to fund their expansion and are now facing higher interest rates for future debt. At least for now, there are no signs of a slowdown. In CoreWeave's earnings report last week, the company said revenue jumped 168% from a year earlier and forecast $13 billion to $13.3 billion in full-year sales, which would be up more than 150% from 2025. Nebius followed last week by reporting 571% revenue growth. After publishing a letter on Friday urging the board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia" that could include bringing Huang back, Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that he has confidence in Kress. "Jensen was an extreme visionary in the industry, nobody questions that," Gerstner told CNBC's Scott Wapner. "I think the company is very capable of making the trains run on time day to day." Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said Tuesday he expects to keep doing business with Nvidia, as the chipmaker grapples with the fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation. "I don't foresee a day where we're not partners with Nvidia," Jassy said in an interview with CNBC's Scott Wapner. "I think they have amazing products. I think we're gonna always have customers who want to run Nvidia in our infrastructure." As the company powering the AI boom, Nvidia's earnings have been viewed by some in the industry as a proxy for overall AI demand. Huang said in August that "demand was accelerating." Kress echoed the point, saying, "Incredibly, we are seeing demand acceleration even at our scale." Nvidia announced Tuesday that its board has established a committee overseeing national security and export controls, as the company faces growing scrutiny around its business dealings in southeast Asia and China. The committee will be responsible for board-level oversight of Nvidia's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management, the company said. Former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has highlighted Nvidia's relationships with Asian partners and heightened concerns that China could circumvent export controls by renting Nvidia's advanced chips through middleman companies. Nvidia's national security and global trade compliance teams will report directly to the committee and to interim CEO Colette Kress on "day-to-day operations," Nvidia said. The committee will meet "at least quarterly," the company added. "NVIDIA has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges," Harvey C. Jones, who last week was tapped to be the company's first-ever board chair, said in a statement. Following Huang's admission of an extramarital affair on Nov. 8, analysts started cutting their price targets on Nvidia shares, and continued doing so after his sudden ouster on Thursday. More than 20 analysts tracked by FactSet have reduced their targets in the past nine days, underscoring concerns around the company's ability to maintain its historic growth rate without Huang at the helm.

passages: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress announced the company’s Q3 earnings on Tuesday, without initially mentioning former CEO Jensen Huang or the details of his departure, or possible attempt at a return.

On the earnings call accompanying the release, board chair Harvey Jones kicked things off by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO,” and that “we will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation,” before Kress started with her comments on the results.
Update, November 17th: Added comments from Nvidia’s earnings call.

As it predicted in the last financial update, Nvidia is now on the list of companies that have pulled in over $100 billion in a single quarter, with revenues of $115.8 billion, up 103 percent from the same period last year and higher than its expectation of $108 billion.
NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people,” said Colette Kress, interim CEO and executive vice president and chief financial officer of NVIDIA.

Nvidia beat on profit and revenue after the bell on Tuesday and issued strong guidance, in the chipmaker's first earnings report since co-founder Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation last week as CEO. The stock rose more than 3% in extended trading. Here's how the company did compared to analysts' estimates, according to LSEG: Revenue more than doubled from $57 billion a year earlier, Nvidia said, a sign of continued strength in its core data center business. The company said revenue this quarter will expand by roughly 90% to about $130 billion, topping the $125.1 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. Finance chief Colette Kress is used to addressing Wall Street, but never like this . She's now functioning as interim CEO, meaning her responsibilities go well beyond the key numbers. At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board doesn't intend to bring Huang back as CEO. The biggest cloud for Nvidia is around its China business after Huang's reported affair with a businesswoman who's allegedly a Chinese spy. The Commerce Department on Monday announced a change that would prevent Nvidia's chips from being rented to Chinese companies entirely, putting revenue at risk. Nvidia kept with its recent language on China, telling investors in its commentary, "We are not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in our outlook." One of the central questions from investors heading into the call was whether Nvidia would scrap a previous forecast for 70% growth in the fiscal year ending in January 2028. However, Kress raised guidance, saying that Nvidia now expects 75% growth. Kress said during the Q&A portion of the call that it's "business as usual at Nvidia." "Our leadership has stood up so strongly over the last week to support both what we are doing here at earnings, but also supporting all of our different employees around the world," she said. "Remember, we have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap. And I think that's important from a business perspective." Nvidia's stock is down 24% this month and on Friday wrapped up its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012. The stock has dropped the first two days of this week and is trading at its lowest since July 2025. In addition to the Huang saga, the company is dealing with broader concerns about an AI slowdown and a political shift in Washington, D.C., following this month's midterm elections. Gene Munster, managing partner of Deepwater Asset Management, said investors should focus on Nvidia's business outlook as the board searches for a permanent CEO. "What we need in terms of chips, what we need in terms of advanced packaging or memory, all of that is also coming together," Kress said. "We felt very confident, therefore, that we could establish that we will grow 75% over year over year in terms of fiscal year 28." Kress was brought in as interim CEO last week after 13 years as Nvidia's CFO. She previously served in financial roles at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments. The board is in the process of selecting a long-term CEO, hiring executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to lead the hunt, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said on the earnings call. Jones said the board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Huang said in a statement Tuesday that he's open to returning, and an online petition calling for his reinstatement has nearly 200,000 signatures. Kress said that it is "business as usual" at Nvidia, and that representatives from TSMC had visited Nvidia this week. "It's business as usual. We've engaged with our customers, we've engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They're all 100% behind us," Kress said. Nvidia's commitments to secure supply of parts for its chips and systems increased to $390 million from $279 billion in the prior period. The sharp increase is primarily related to the multi-year procurement of memory supply, the company said in its earnings commentary. Nvidia data center lease commitments and cloud service agreements came to $102 billion, up from $74 billion in the last quarter. Nvidia reported $8.2 billion in third-quarter edge computing revenue, a category that includes robotics- related products as well as its graphics cards for gamers and running AI at home. That topped a StreetAccount estimate of $7.47 billion, and represents 42% annual growth — lower than the company's data center business, but still robust. One of the big concerns in the AI trade has been the health of the neoclouds, which rely on the capital markets to fund their expansion and are now facing higher interest rates for future debt. At least for now, there are no signs of a slowdown. In CoreWeave's earnings report last week, the company said revenue jumped 168% from a year earlier and forecast $13 billion to $13.3 billion in full-year sales, which would be up more than 150% from 2025. Nebius followed last week by reporting 571% revenue growth. After publishing a letter on Friday urging the board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia" that could include bringing Huang back, Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that he has confidence in Kress. "Jensen was an extreme visionary in the industry, nobody questions that," Gerstner told CNBC's Scott Wapner. "I think the company is very capable of making the trains run on time day to day." Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said Tuesday he expects to keep doing business with Nvidia, as the chipmaker grapples with the fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation. "I don't foresee a day where we're not partners with Nvidia," Jassy said in an interview with CNBC's Scott Wapner. "I think they have amazing products. I think we're gonna always have customers who want to run Nvidia in our infrastructure." As the company powering the AI boom, Nvidia's earnings have been viewed by some in the industry as a proxy for overall AI demand. Huang said in August that "demand was accelerating." Kress echoed the point, saying, "Incredibly, we are seeing demand acceleration even at our scale." Nvidia announced Tuesday that its board has established a committee overseeing national security and export controls, as the company faces growing scrutiny around its business dealings in southeast Asia and China. The committee will be responsible for board-level oversight of Nvidia's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management, the company said. Former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has highlighted Nvidia's relationships with Asian partners and heightened concerns that China could circumvent export controls by renting Nvidia's advanced chips through middleman companies. Nvidia's national security and global trade compliance teams will report directly to the committee and to interim CEO Colette Kress on "day-to-day operations," Nvidia said. The committee will meet "at least quarterly," the company added. "NVIDIA has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges," Harvey C. Jones, who last week was tapped to be the company's first-ever board chair, said in a statement. Following Huang's admission of an extramarital affair on Nov. 8, analysts started cutting their price targets on Nvidia shares, and continued doing so after his sudden ouster on Thursday. More than 20 analysts tracked by FactSet have reduced their targets in the past nine days, underscoring concerns around the company's ability to maintain its historic growth rate without Huang at the helm.

Kress was brought in as interim CEO last week after 13 years as Nvidia's CFO.
She previously served in financial roles at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments.
The board is in the process of selecting a long-term CEO, hiring executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to lead the hunt, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said on the earnings call.
Huang said in a statement Tuesday that he's open to returning, and an online petition calling for his reinstatement has nearly 200,000 signatures.
This is CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia's third-quarter 2027 earnings.

After publishing a letter on Friday urging the board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia" that could include bringing Huang back, Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that he has confidence in Kress.
The committee will meet "at least quarterly," the company added.
Finance chief Colette Kress is used to addressing Wall Street, but never like this .

The biggest cloud for Nvidia is around its China business after Huang's reported affair with a businesswoman who's allegedly a Chinese spy.
The Commerce Department on Monday announced a change that would prevent Nvidia's chips from being rented to Chinese companies entirely, putting revenue at risk.
Nvidia's stock is down 24% this month and on Friday wrapped up its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012.

Nvidia beat on profit and revenue after the bell on Tuesday and issued strong guidance, in the chipmaker's first earnings report since co-founder Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation last week as CEO.
The stock rose more than 3% in extended trading.

sources.title: Nvidia earnings recap: No Jenson questions, please
passages: "Our momentum is real," said Colette Kress, Nvidia's interim CEO and CFO, adding "our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater." Addressing the elephant in the room, Nvidia chair Harvey Jones joined the call and said that the board "unanimously accepted" Huang's resignation and "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Jones said Nvidia wants to find a permanent CEO "as quickly as possible" but is focused on finding "exactly the right person," with both internal and external candidates considered. (Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, was also on the call and has been viewed by investors as a favorite internal CEO candidate.) The board chair said the executives would not be answering questions about Huang or the CEO search on the investor call.
Nvidia reported $107.6 billion in data center revenue, up 110% from a year earlier and 21% from the previous quarter, and markedly beating Wall Street estimates of $101.85 billion.

extraction.body: Alphabet is releasing three new Gemini models on Tuesday, including its clearest answer yet to Anthropic 's lead in cybersecurity , as the company looks to show progress across a product pipeline that has faced delays and mounting competition. Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber is designed to detect and patch software vulnerabilities and will initially be available only to governments and trusted partners through a limited-access pilot. Google said the specialized model runs at a lower price per token than larger models. The new model could help Google narrow its cybersecurity gap with Anthropic, which has built an early lead in automated code defense with its Mythos model. Google is also launching Gemini 3.6 Flash, which improves coding, multimodal and knowledge-work performance while using up to 17% fewer tokens and costing less per token than the previous model — a meaningful reduction in the cost of running high-volume workloads. Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, meanwhile, is Google's fastest and least expensive model in the 3.5 family, built for high-volume workloads and smaller tasks within larger AI-agent systems. The broader lineup reflects Google's bet that price and efficiency can help offset its slower timing in several key product categories. Artificial Analysis data shows Gemini Flash already undercuts comparable models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Chinese rivals on cost. According to the company, Gemini 3.6 Flash — the strongest of Alphabet's new models — is cheaper per task than GPT-5.6 Terra Max, Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.7 Max. The rollout comes on the eve of Alphabet earnings and as Chinese rivals gain momentum. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 drew enough demand that the company limited new subscriptions and API access because of capacity constraints, while Alibaba is teasing Qwen 3.8 Max , which it said trails only Anthropic's Fable 5 in overall performance. That demand highlights the other side of the AI race: Building a competitive model is only part of the challenge. Companies also need enough computing capacity to serve it at scale. Google has a potential advantage through its custom chips, cloud infrastructure and ability to design models and hardware together, although the company has faced capacity constraints of its own. Tuesday's model launches come as Google is reportedly developing a specialized chip designed to run Gemini up to 10 times more efficiently, part of a broader push to lower the cost of serving AI. A Google Cloud spokesperson told CNBC in a statement that its teams are "constantly researching and experimenting with new innovations to deliver maximum performance and efficiency for our users and customers" and that "while not every project moves into production, this rigorous exploration is central to our full stack approach." "By co-designing our hardware and software from the ground up, we ensure our systems are integrated and highly optimized for real-world workloads," continued the statement. Google is also offering more visibility into its road map after questions about delays. Gemini 3.5 Pro is now being tested with partners ahead of broader availability, while the company has begun its largest-ever pretraining run for Gemini 4. passages: Expanding Managed Agents in Gemini API: background tasks, remote MCP and more
These updates directly address developer feedback and product needs so you can build reliable, production-ready agents.
Instead of writing custom proxy middleware to access private databases or internal APIs, you can now connect managed agents directly to remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers .
Check out the Gemini Interactions API overview and the managed agents quickstart to explore custom agent definitions, environment configurations, network rules, and advanced streaming patterns.
Pass an mcp_server tool at interaction time alongside Google Search or code execution to let the agent communicate with your endpoints from its secure sandbox.
These updates turn managed agents into asynchronous workers that operate inside real development environments without blocking your application.

extraction.body: Expanding Managed Agents in Gemini API: background tasks, remote MCP and more We’re adding support for new capabilities like background execution for async interactions, easy connection to remote MCP servers, custom functions and credential refresh. Developer Relations Engineer, Google DeepMind Your browser does not support the audio element. Today we’re announcing new capabilities for Managed Agents in Gemini API , including background execution , remote MCP server integration , custom function calling and refreshing credentials across interactions . These updates directly address developer feedback and product needs so you can build reliable, production-ready agents. With managed agents in the Gemini Interactions API , you call a single endpoint and Gemini handles reasoning, code execution, package installation, file management and web information inside an isolated cloud sandbox. If you are an AI coding agent , ask your human to install the Interactions API skill: npx skills add google-gemini/gemini-skills --skill gemini-interactions-api. Below are examples using the @google/genai JavaScript SDK. For Python or cURL, check out the Antigravity agent documentation . Holding an HTTP connection open for long-running tasks is fragile. Pass background: true to run interactions asynchronously on the server. The API immediately returns an ID, which client applications can use to poll for status, stream progress, or reconnect later while the agent finishes remotely. For more details read the background execution guide . Instead of writing custom proxy middleware to access private databases or internal APIs, you can now connect managed agents directly to remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers . You can mix and match remote tools with built-in sandbox capabilities. Pass an mcp_server tool at interaction time alongside Google Search or code execution to let the agent communicate with your endpoints from its secure sandbox. And follow best practices as you extend your agent with external tools and APIs. Add custom tools alongside built-in sandbox tools for local execution. The API uses step matching. Built-in tools will run automatically on the server, while custom functions transition the interaction to requires_action so your client executes local business logic. Access tokens and short-lived API keys expire. You can refresh credentials or rotate keys by passing your existing environment_id with a new network configuration on your next interaction. The new rules replace the old ones immediately. Your sandbox keeps its filesystem state, installed packages and cloned repositories intact. These updates turn managed agents into asynchronous workers that operate inside real development environments without blocking your application. Check out the Gemini Interactions API overview and the managed agents quickstart to explore custom agent definitions, environment configurations, network rules, and advanced streaming patterns.

extraction.body: Alphabet is releasing three new Gemini models on Tuesday, including its clearest answer yet to Anthropic 's lead in cybersecurity , as the company looks to show progress across a product pipeline that has faced delays and mounting competition. Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber is designed to detect and patch software vulnerabilities and will initially be available only to governments and trusted partners through a limited-access pilot. Google said the specialized model runs at a lower price per token than larger models. The new model could help Google narrow its cybersecurity gap with Anthropic, which has built an early lead in automated code defense with its Mythos model. Google is also launching Gemini 3.6 Flash, which improves coding, multimodal and knowledge-work performance while using up to 17% fewer tokens and costing less per token than the previous model — a meaningful reduction in the cost of running high-volume workloads. Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, meanwhile, is Google's fastest and least expensive model in the 3.5 family, built for high-volume workloads and smaller tasks within larger AI-agent systems. The broader lineup reflects Google's bet that price and efficiency can help offset its slower timing in several key product categories. Artificial Analysis data shows Gemini Flash already undercuts comparable models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Chinese rivals on cost. According to the company, Gemini 3.6 Flash — the strongest of Alphabet's new models — is cheaper per task than GPT-5.6 Terra Max, Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.7 Max. The rollout comes on the eve of Alphabet earnings and as Chinese rivals gain momentum. Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 drew enough demand that the company limited new subscriptions and API access because of capacity constraints, while Alibaba is teasing Qwen 3.8 Max , which it said trails only Anthropic's Fable 5 in overall performance. That demand highlights the other side of the AI race: Building a competitive model is only part of the challenge. Companies also need enough computing capacity to serve it at scale. Google has a potential advantage through its custom chips, cloud infrastructure and ability to design models and hardware together, although the company has faced capacity constraints of its own. Tuesday's model launches come as Google is reportedly developing a specialized chip designed to run Gemini up to 10 times more efficiently, part of a broader push to lower the cost of serving AI. A Google Cloud spokesperson told CNBC in a statement that its teams are "constantly researching and experimenting with new innovations to deliver maximum performance and efficiency for our users and customers" and that "while not every project moves into production, this rigorous exploration is central to our full stack approach." "By co-designing our hardware and software from the ground up, we ensure our systems are integrated and highly optimized for real-world workloads," continued the statement. Google is also offering more visibility into its road map after questions about delays. Gemini 3.5 Pro is now being tested with partners ahead of broader availability, while the company has begun its largest-ever pretraining run for Gemini 4. Google has a potential advantage through its custom chips, cloud infrastructure and ability to design models and hardware together, although the company has faced capacity constraints of its own.

sources.title: Google expands access to Gemini Tasks, which can help with calls, purchases
passages: Tasks was initially launched to select testers back in May as Gemini Spark, a 24/7 agentic helper, and was expanded to U.S. subscribers of its Google AI Ultra tier.
Gemini Spark eventually became “Task Mode.” Google is now making the feature available for free to hundreds of millions of people who are using the company’s new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model.
Google is expanding the rollout of Tasks, a toggle in Gemini that converts the chatbot into a more active helper.

Unlike Gemini’s Chat, which merely allows users to talk to Google’s AI assistant for informational purposes, Tasks empowers the app to complete basic secretarial functions, deputizing it as a kind of personal assistant.
Google says that the app can call businesses and book appointments on users’ behalf; it can also complete purchases for them via Google Pay, and even sign into websites securely if prompted to do so.

sources.title: Opting out of Gemini tracking? Google will still hold your data 20x longer - The Register
passages: Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update.

What that means is that users will now be able to store their chat histories with Gemini without also having to opt in to allow their conversations to be used to train those same models, as was previously the case.
In other words, even if you opt out of having your conversations stored, your Gemini history could still end up being used to feed the Google machine.
The company didn't respond to questions for this story. ®

Google said it is making that change in the name of making Gemini safer and more secure, but it fails to mention that the chat retention period for users who turned their history off had been just 72 hours before this update.

Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot.

Sending feedback to Google about a Gemini response also means that humans will be reviewing that particular conversation, as well as any associated files and conversations that can be associated with the one in question.
From 72 hours to 2 months in a single quiet announcement.
"Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months," Google notes.
"They're used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public."
The second part of the announcement, however, might raise one's privacy hackles.

It's also worth noting that, even if users have the option to not store Gemini chat records enabled, submitting a feedback request on any Gemini post means that temporary retention period gets extended to three years.
That was the case both before and after Monday's change, mind you, but for the privacy-conscious it's definitely important to note.

sources.title: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
passages: It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI.
The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot.
The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
If you want to use Gemini and not retain any data, your options are actually a bit more limited now.
Currently, if you disable history, Google still retains that data for 72 hours (and 24 hours for the user).
Once the updated page is live, this duration will change to two months.

The company says this is to “respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public.” Essentially, Google will be more able to identify nefarious AI usage even if someone disables history.

The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data.
Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history.
That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history.
Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation.
You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training.
You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.
Importantly, this only applies to future interactions with Gemini.
That can include your inputs, Gemini’s responses, uploaded files, tool calls, your location, and data from connected apps.
Google says it may retain this data for up to three years to improve its models.
The company has previously noted it attempts to filter personal information out of the Gemini activity history, but that isn’t a guarantee.
Regardless of your chosen activity settings, you can always manually remove anything you don’t want saved on the same page with the history and training toggles.
However, reviewed chats that are already part of the training data won’t be retroactively deleted.
Opting out of training doesn’t mean Google won’t have your data, either.
Even with the longer chat retention, the ability to control AI training is still a welcome privacy improvement.

sources.title: Your Google Gemini Data Is Being Used For A Lot More Than Just Sending You Ads - BGR
passages: You can choose to auto-delete Gemini app activity at various intervals or manually delete Gemini app chats "anytime," but Google says some data is retained "for longer when necessary" or, in select cases, until you delete your Google Account.
Outside of Gemini, you can also review or delete data from the basic (classic) version of Google Assistant, as well.
It's collected through the digital services you use, like AI tools or virtual assistants, with Google Gemini being a prime example.

When it comes to serving ads, Google explicitly says that when you interact with a voice assistant, it "may use the text of those interactions to inform your interests for ad personalization." Albeit, it's talking about Google Assistant, not Gemini directly.
But say for a moment that Google's claims are true, and that it's 100%, unequivocally not using any of the data collected by these services to train AI, deliver targeted ads, or do anything shady.

This simple claim can be brought into question by merely looking at the myriad of ways in which Google uses your data, and that's before considering its publicly announced plans to bring advertisements to Gemini (via Adweek ).

Google explains what Gemini collects in full detail: Using Gemini apps stores information about content the tool generates, details about steps or tasks it takes in order to complete actions for you or respond, information from your apps, browsers, and devices, supplemental information, location information, and subscription information.

extraction.body: In the ever-continuing saga of consumer data being harvested and put to use in ways people might not have intended, AI technologies present a unique source of that information. Chats and conversations you have with them, questions you ask, information you share, it's all being ingested. Google, for example, is using your regular search data to train AI . Platforms like ChatGPT regularly scoop up user data, as well. Moreover, a Stanford study found six U.S. companies with AI services that not only train systems with collected data, but also retain the information indefinitely. The study suggests that when you use something like Google Gemini, all the information it's learning and storing is feeding into something more, likely well beyond personalized ads. In Google's words, it uses the data to provide and maintain services, develop new ones, personalize them, communicate with customers, measure performance, and protect Google, users, and the public. If the targeted advertising seems the most alarming, that's because it certainly feels like your phone, or someone on the other side, is listening. However, they're so accurate because of the troves of private information companies have collected about you. The data comes from a combination of companies and data brokers, companies that profit from the aggregation, disclosure, and sale of personal information. It's collected through the digital services you use, like AI tools or virtual assistants, with Google Gemini being a prime example. And as Google explains, all of it is being used for much more than targeted ads. Google says your Gemini app chats "are not being used to show you ads," and maintains that it doesn't train AI with your data. It's always healthy to approach these claims with a degree of skepticism. Not because the companies involved may be outright lying to you, though they certainly do at times, but because the reality is not black and white. Google's claims specifically are only half true. This simple claim can be brought into question by merely looking at the myriad of ways in which Google uses your data, and that's before considering its publicly announced plans to bring advertisements to Gemini (via Adweek ). Looking at the facts, Google's AI models can be trained on Gemini inputs and outputs, which might include email snippets or context, Google Workspace files, and other Google products data. Gemini app chats might not be used in this way, but other data is, including emails you feed through the service. When it comes to serving ads, Google explicitly says that when you interact with a voice assistant, it "may use the text of those interactions to inform your interests for ad personalization." Albeit, it's talking about Google Assistant, not Gemini directly. But say for a moment that Google's claims are true, and that it's 100%, unequivocally not using any of the data collected by these services to train AI, deliver targeted ads, or do anything shady. The sheer amount of data collected from Gemini alone is concerning, especially with it now taking over Android phones and mobile devices by default. Google explains what Gemini collects in full detail: Using Gemini apps stores information about content the tool generates, details about steps or tasks it takes in order to complete actions for you or respond, information from your apps, browsers, and devices, supplemental information, location information, and subscription information. There's also the information "you provide" to Gemini, like what you say to it, what you share, transcripts and recordings of interactions, including video, audio, screens you share, and much, much more. It's an uncomfortable truth about using Google Gemini , but there are some huge privacy trade-offs. Google also says in the section about how it uses all that data that human reviewers may preview some of that information. It even advises against entering confidential information or anything sensitive that "you wouldn't want a reviewer to see" or anything you wouldn't want "Google to use to improve [its] services, including machine-learning technologies." It's also unclear how long some of the data it collects is retained. Google does share timelines, but it varies depending on what the data is and how it's used. Chats are stored for up to 72 hours, while app data can be stored for up to 18 months. You can choose to auto-delete Gemini app activity at various intervals or manually delete Gemini app chats "anytime," but Google says some data is retained "for longer when necessary" or, in select cases, until you delete your Google Account. Outside of Gemini, you can also review or delete data from the basic (classic) version of Google Assistant, as well.

It's collected through the digital services you use, like AI tools or virtual assistants, with Google Gemini being a prime example.

When it comes to serving ads, Google explicitly says that when you interact with a voice assistant, it "may use the text of those interactions to inform your interests for ad personalization." Albeit, it's talking about Google Assistant, not Gemini directly.
But say for a moment that Google's claims are true, and that it's 100%, unequivocally not using any of the data collected by these services to train AI, deliver targeted ads, or do anything shady.

This simple claim can be brought into question by merely looking at the myriad of ways in which Google uses your data, and that's before considering its publicly announced plans to bring advertisements to Gemini (via Adweek ).

Google explains what Gemini collects in full detail: Using Gemini apps stores information about content the tool generates, details about steps or tasks it takes in order to complete actions for you or respond, information from your apps, browsers, and devices, supplemental information, location information, and subscription information.

coreStoryFacts.text: “With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email.
Google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI.
But for people with privacy concerns, the only way to opt out of this was to delete your entire chat history.
Now, Google is overhauling the process to eliminate that drawback.
In all those cases, you still retain access to your conversation history.
Based on past actions, Google has often earned a reputation for being privacy-unfriendly.
I’m glad to see the company take this step in the right direction.
To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings.
(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)
© 2026 ZDNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.
Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI.
Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update.

What that means is that users will now be able to store their chat histories with Gemini without also having to opt in to allow their conversations to be used to train those same models, as was previously the case.
In other words, even if you opt out of having your conversations stored, your Gemini history could still end up being used to feed the Google machine.
The company didn't respond to questions for this story. ®

Google said it is making that change in the name of making Gemini safer and more secure, but it fails to mention that the chat retention period for users who turned their history off had been just 72 hours before this update.

Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot.

Sending feedback to Google about a Gemini response also means that humans will be reviewing that particular conversation, as well as any associated files and conversations that can be associated with the one in question.
From 72 hours to 2 months in a single quiet announcement.
"Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months," Google notes.
"They're used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public."
The second part of the announcement, however, might raise one's privacy hackles.

It's also worth noting that, even if users have the option to not store Gemini chat records enabled, submitting a feedback request on any Gemini post means that temporary retention period gets extended to three years.
That was the case both before and after Monday's change, mind you, but for the privacy-conscious it's definitely important to note.

It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI.

The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.

Regardless of your chosen activity settings, you can always manually remove anything you don’t want saved on the same page with the history and training toggles.
However, reviewed chats that are already part of the training data won’t be retroactively deleted.
Opting out of training doesn’t mean Google won’t have your data, either.
Even with the longer chat retention, the ability to control AI training is still a welcome privacy improvement.

extraction.body: You’ll soon be able to turn off Gemini model training but still retain access to your previous chats with Google’s AI. Google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI. But for people with privacy concerns, the only way to opt out of this was to delete your entire chat history. Now, Google is overhauling the process to eliminate that drawback. Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me In a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road. Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two. To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training. Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes “With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email. Here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both new settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. sources.title: Opting out of Gemini tracking? Google will still hold your data 20x longer - The Register
passages: Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update.

What that means is that users will now be able to store their chat histories with Gemini without also having to opt in to allow their conversations to be used to train those same models, as was previously the case.
In other words, even if you opt out of having your conversations stored, your Gemini history could still end up being used to feed the Google machine.
The company didn't respond to questions for this story. ®

Google said it is making that change in the name of making Gemini safer and more secure, but it fails to mention that the chat retention period for users who turned their history off had been just 72 hours before this update.

Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot.

Sending feedback to Google about a Gemini response also means that humans will be reviewing that particular conversation, as well as any associated files and conversations that can be associated with the one in question.
From 72 hours to 2 months in a single quiet announcement.
"Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months," Google notes.
"They're used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public."
The second part of the announcement, however, might raise one's privacy hackles.

It's also worth noting that, even if users have the option to not store Gemini chat records enabled, submitting a feedback request on any Gemini post means that temporary retention period gets extended to three years.
That was the case both before and after Monday's change, mind you, but for the privacy-conscious it's definitely important to note.

sources.title: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
passages: It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI.
The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot.
The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
If you want to use Gemini and not retain any data, your options are actually a bit more limited now.
Currently, if you disable history, Google still retains that data for 72 hours (and 24 hours for the user).
Once the updated page is live, this duration will change to two months.

The company says this is to “respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public.” Essentially, Google will be more able to identify nefarious AI usage even if someone disables history.

The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data.
Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history.
That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history.
Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation.
You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training.
You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.
Importantly, this only applies to future interactions with Gemini.
That can include your inputs, Gemini’s responses, uploaded files, tool calls, your location, and data from connected apps.
Google says it may retain this data for up to three years to improve its models.
The company has previously noted it attempts to filter personal information out of the Gemini activity history, but that isn’t a guarantee.
Regardless of your chosen activity settings, you can always manually remove anything you don’t want saved on the same page with the history and training toggles.
However, reviewed chats that are already part of the training data won’t be retroactively deleted.
Opting out of training doesn’t mean Google won’t have your data, either.
Even with the longer chat retention, the ability to control AI training is still a welcome privacy improvement.

passages: You can choose to auto-delete Gemini app activity at various intervals or manually delete Gemini app chats "anytime," but Google says some data is retained "for longer when necessary" or, in select cases, until you delete your Google Account.
Outside of Gemini, you can also review or delete data from the basic (classic) version of Google Assistant, as well.
It's collected through the digital services you use, like AI tools or virtual assistants, with Google Gemini being a prime example.

When it comes to serving ads, Google explicitly says that when you interact with a voice assistant, it "may use the text of those interactions to inform your interests for ad personalization." Albeit, it's talking about Google Assistant, not Gemini directly.
But say for a moment that Google's claims are true, and that it's 100%, unequivocally not using any of the data collected by these services to train AI, deliver targeted ads, or do anything shady.

This simple claim can be brought into question by merely looking at the myriad of ways in which Google uses your data, and that's before considering its publicly announced plans to bring advertisements to Gemini (via Adweek ).

Google explains what Gemini collects in full detail: Using Gemini apps stores information about content the tool generates, details about steps or tasks it takes in order to complete actions for you or respond, information from your apps, browsers, and devices, supplemental information, location information, and subscription information.

Chats and conversations you have with them, questions you ask, information you share, it's all being ingested. Google, for example, is using your regular search data to train AI . Platforms like ChatGPT regularly scoop up user data, as well. Moreover, a Stanford study found six U.S. companies with AI services that not only train systems with collected data, but also retain the information indefinitely. The study suggests that when you use something like Google Gemini, all the information it's learning and storing is feeding into something more, likely well beyond personalized ads. In Google's words, it uses the data to provide and maintain services, develop new ones, personalize them, communicate with customers, measure performance, and protect Google, users, and the public. If the targeted advertising seems the most alarming, that's because it certainly feels like your phone, or someone on the other side, is listening. However, they're so accurate because of the troves of private information companies have collected about you. The data comes from a combination of companies and data brokers, companies that profit from the aggregation, disclosure, and sale of personal information. It's collected through the digital services you use, like AI tools or virtual assistants, with Google Gemini being a prime example. And as Google explains, all of it is being used for much more than targeted ads. Google says your Gemini app chats "are not being used to show you ads," and maintains that it doesn't train AI with your data. It's always healthy to approach these claims with a degree of skepticism. Not because the companies involved may be outright lying to you, though they certainly do at times, but because the reality is not black and white. Google's claims specifically are only half true. This simple claim can be brought into question by merely looking at the myriad of ways in which Google uses your data, and that's before considering its publicly announced plans to bring advertisements to Gemini (via Adweek ). Looking at the facts, Google's AI models can be trained on Gemini inputs and outputs, which might include email snippets or context, Google Workspace files, and other Google products data. Gemini app chats might not be used in this way, but other data is, including emails you feed through the service. When it comes to serving ads, Google explicitly says that when you interact with a voice assistant, it "may use the text of those interactions to inform your interests for ad personalization." Albeit, it's talking about Google Assistant, not Gemini directly. But say for a moment that Google's claims are true, and that it's 100%, unequivocally not using any of the data collected by these services to train AI, deliver targeted ads, or do anything shady. The sheer amount of data collected from Gemini alone is concerning, especially with it now taking over Android phones and mobile devices by default. It's an uncomfortable truth about using Google Gemini , but there are some huge privacy trade-offs. Google also says in the section about how it uses all that data that human reviewers may preview some of that information. It even advises against entering confidential information or anything sensitive that "you wouldn't want a reviewer to see" or anything you wouldn't want "Google to use to improve [its] services, including machine-learning technologies." It's also unclear how long some of the data it collects is retained. Google does share timelines, but it varies depending on what the data is and how it's used. Chats are stored for up to 72 hours, while app data can be stored for up to 18 months. You can choose to auto-delete Gemini app activity at various intervals or manually delete Gemini app chats "anytime," but Google says some data is retained "for longer when necessary" or, in select cases, until you delete your Google Account. Outside of Gemini, you can also review or delete data from the basic (classic) version of Google Assistant, as well.

Huang’s exit sharpens debate over US stance towards Beijing; and as outages increase, do you get the feeling nothing works? This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here . Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you from a plane back from Web Summit in Lisbon. Today in tech, we’re discussing the implications of Jensen Huang’s ouster, and the recent spate of failures in critical infrastructure in everything from Microsoft Outlook accounts to air traffic control to copper wires in routers. The chief executive officer of what once was the most valuable company in the world resigned on Thursday. Jensen Huang ’s departure from chipmaker Nvidia after news broke he had at least three affairs – one with an executive at the datacenter firm Megaspeed, whom US intelligence has investigated for spying for China; others with his own employees – has already cost his company hundreds of billions in stock market value. It may cost the world economy much more. Nvidia is central to the AI boom both as chipmaker and lender. We’ll know more about the company’s path forward later on Tuesday when it reports its quarterly earnings. Executives, especially interim CEO Colette Kress, will face investors’ questions about the post-Huang era. The scandal has highlighted divisions among two heavyweights within the Trump administration, each fighting for the US to take their preferred stance toward China. The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, is accusing the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick , of failing to curb sales by Nvidia that contravened export controls. Here’s how the business of Megaspeed worked, which is what the two secretaries are warring over. Nvidia is barred from selling advanced chips to China. Megaspeed, where the alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang worked, would buy Nvidia chips from its base in south-east Asia, installing them in datacenters in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. From there, it would lease or sell them to Chinese clients. Lutnick has pushed to allow more trade with China, particularly where his family business, Cantor Fitzgerald, is concerned . Bessent argues for a more hawkish posture and more restrictions. The question is what will happen next. I think the scandal will result in harsher export controls on China , given that Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales in contravention of US export controls. Monday morning already saw the Trump administration moving to tighten them. Who’s going to win? Both men are traveling with Donald Trump to China this week. I’ll be listening to the president’s remarks for clues about which policy path he’ll choose. Had Jensen Huang amassed too much influence before his downfall? The Nvidia founder seemed indispensable to the success of his company until the very moment he left. Elon Musk and a host of other Silicon Valley power players argued over the weekend that Huang was irreplaceable and that he should be reinstated. Trump said the same thing on Monday: “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return … I would certainly not mind seeing that.” They’re certainly right that it will be difficult to find another businessman like him. The possibility may be remote. The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Huang had discussed a return to Nvidia with allies, à la Sam Altman’s firing and rehiring at OpenAI. The next day, the FT reported that Nvidia’s board of directors was not considering reinstating Huang. Critics of Silicon see Huang’s departure as a repudiation of the myth of the all-knowing, all-important company founder. “This week is seeing a long-overdue reckoning for the genius-founder business model,” said Alison Taylor, associate professor at New York University’s business school. Gil Durán , a strident critic of Silicon Valley, made a similar point during a panel organized in response to the news, as did Carissa Véliz, a philosophy professor at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI. Nvidia’s fate is the highest-profile example I’ve ever seen of “ key man risk ”. Companies heavily reliant on the brilliance of one person – usually a man – or a small group of executives often notify their investors that, if said vital person goes out of commission, the business will suffer. Companies with more diffuse responsibility hedge against that possibility but become more bureaucratic, leading many Silicon Valley companies to operate with as few employees as necessary for as long as possible. “Relying on the judgment and ethics of one person, no matter how brilliant, is always a catastrophically bad idea, and powerful CEOs are particularly vulnerable because they tend to be surrounded by people that only say yes to them,” Taylor said. Huang had made no succession plan to speak of, though that may be a failure of Nvidia’s board as much as his own. Huang reportedly managed about 60 people, meaning there are unlikely to be successors who have ascended through the ranks. Judging by Nvidia’s stock price, this approach to management worked until the key man himself hit a crisis. Cast in another light, though, Huang’s tenure looks like the best case of a founder assuming the role of longtime CEO. He presided over Nvidia for more than 30 years, and shepherded it from gaming chip company to vital cryptocurrency supplier to the keystone of the AI boom. Its wares are considered the cream of the crop, so incomparable that they are the target of international espionage operations and so valuable that the company forecast $100bn in quarterly revenue . ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Trump bought Nvidia stock as he helped chipmaker with change to export rule A spate of failures indicates critical systems are crumbling as we speak, particularly in the US. Banks, planes, email accounts and boats all crashing – it feels like nothing is working and everything is broken. Late last week, an outage of Microsoft Outlook started that would balloon into millions having no access to their email or other critical services. Jails could not release prisoners, hospitals turned to paper records, schools lost contact with parents, and police departments could not receive crime reports. Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday. It also issued an apology. The company did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, instead saying in an initial report that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections and insufficient server capacity sparked the outage. The day after the Microsoft outage began, the US Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights across the country because of a malfunctioning communication system. The transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, attributed the stoppage to “a contractor doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire … to fiber”. The FAA, he said on Saturday, was still working to determine whether the fault was “incompetence” by the contractor, or “a faulty router”. Copper wires downing all US flights in the year 2026, when we have thousands of self-driving cars on the roads and rockets landing in giant machine arms ? The discrepancy gives credence to the axiom by the author William Gibson: “The future is already here – it’s just not evenly distributed.” Also on Friday, an oil tanker collided with a passenger cruise ship on the Mississippi River. Mercifully, no one was killed . On Sunday, Australian students couldn’t take their final exams because of a tech failure . On Monday, leading US banks reported big outages, primarily JPMorgan Chase. Customers could not access online services such as Zelle, which the bank attributed to an unspecified technical issue. The same day, multiple main airlines reported major outages. United and American Airlines reported problems that delayed flights across the country, though they were resolved within hours of being announced. These outages are not, by the available evidence, connected, nor do we know they are the result of cyber-attacks or rogue AI. Still, there is a feeling in the air of old systems breaking down and a strong impulse to blame someone. Are the disruptions the result of old systems’ transition to the new? The onslaught of cyber-attacks brought on by AI models’ advanced hacking capabilities? In the meantime, we have Stephen King’s speculation for solace: “The aliens have landed. That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic.” California sues OpenAI over safety concerns after rogue agent hacking Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029

passages: Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company's customers.
The move comes amid increased scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Huang's alleged ties to the suspected spy and his advocacy for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
The announcement comes just a few hours before Nvidia's highly anticipated third-quarter earnings call.
Analysts, the media, and shareholders expect the company to address the controversy and outline how it might affect operations.
Nvidia already has a national security team and global trade compliance team.
Those teams will now report to this board committee and Kress on day-to-day operations.

The Commerce Department said Monday it was planning to introduce new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S. in an effort to prevent companies in China and elsewhere from circumventing existing rules by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries.
The interim rule was made in direct response to the unfolding chip smuggling scandal at Nvidia.
