Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company's customers. Nvidia said Tuesday that the new standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. extraction.body: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff. The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.” Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely. Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue. In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change. Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China. That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch. If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share. Huang’s exit sharpens debate over US stance towards Beijing; and as outages increase, do you get the feeling nothing works? This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here . Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you from a plane back from Web Summit in Lisbon. Today in tech, we’re discussing the implications of Jensen Huang’s ouster, and the recent spate of failures in critical infrastructure in everything from Microsoft Outlook accounts to air traffic control to copper wires in routers. The chief executive officer of what once was the most valuable company in the world resigned on Thursday. Jensen Huang ’s departure from chipmaker Nvidia after news broke he had at least three affairs – one with an executive at the datacenter firm Megaspeed, whom US intelligence has investigated for spying for China; others with his own employees – has already cost his company hundreds of billions in stock market value. It may cost the world economy much more. Nvidia is central to the AI boom both as chipmaker and lender. We’ll know more about the company’s path forward later on Tuesday when it reports its quarterly earnings. Executives, especially interim CEO Colette Kress, will face investors’ questions about the post-Huang era. The scandal has highlighted divisions among two heavyweights within the Trump administration, each fighting for the US to take their preferred stance toward China. The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, is accusing the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick , of failing to curb sales by Nvidia that contravened export controls. Here’s how the business of Megaspeed worked, which is what the two secretaries are warring over. Nvidia is barred from selling advanced chips to China. Megaspeed, where the alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang worked, would buy Nvidia chips from its base in south-east Asia, installing them in datacenters in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. From there, it would lease or sell them to Chinese clients. Lutnick has pushed to allow more trade with China, particularly where his family business, Cantor Fitzgerald, is concerned . Bessent argues for a more hawkish posture and more restrictions. The question is what will happen next. I think the scandal will result in harsher export controls on China , given that Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales in contravention of US export controls. Monday morning already saw the Trump administration moving to tighten them. Who’s going to win? Both men are traveling with Donald Trump to China this week. I’ll be listening to the president’s remarks for clues about which policy path he’ll choose. Had Jensen Huang amassed too much influence before his downfall? The Nvidia founder seemed indispensable to the success of his company until the very moment he left. Elon Musk and a host of other Silicon Valley power players argued over the weekend that Huang was irreplaceable and that he should be reinstated. Trump said the same thing on Monday: “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return … I would certainly not mind seeing that.” They’re certainly right that it will be difficult to find another businessman like him. The possibility may be remote. The Financial Times reported on Sunday that Huang had discussed a return to Nvidia with allies, à la Sam Altman’s firing and rehiring at OpenAI. The next day, the FT reported that Nvidia’s board of directors was not considering reinstating Huang. Critics of Silicon see Huang’s departure as a repudiation of the myth of the all-knowing, all-important company founder. “This week is seeing a long-overdue reckoning for the genius-founder business model,” said Alison Taylor, associate professor at New York University’s business school. Gil Durán , a strident critic of Silicon Valley, made a similar point during a panel organized in response to the news, as did Carissa Véliz, a philosophy professor at the Oxford Institute for Ethics in AI. Nvidia’s fate is the highest-profile example I’ve ever seen of “ key man risk ”. Companies heavily reliant on the brilliance of one person – usually a man – or a small group of executives often notify their investors that, if said vital person goes out of commission, the business will suffer. Companies with more diffuse responsibility hedge against that possibility but become more bureaucratic, leading many Silicon Valley companies to operate with as few employees as necessary for as long as possible. “Relying on the judgment and ethics of one person, no matter how brilliant, is always a catastrophically bad idea, and powerful CEOs are particularly vulnerable because they tend to be surrounded by people that only say yes to them,” Taylor said. Huang had made no succession plan to speak of, though that may be a failure of Nvidia’s board as much as his own. Huang reportedly managed about 60 people, meaning there are unlikely to be successors who have ascended through the ranks. Judging by Nvidia’s stock price, this approach to management worked until the key man himself hit a crisis. Cast in another light, though, Huang’s tenure looks like the best case of a founder assuming the role of longtime CEO. He presided over Nvidia for more than 30 years, and shepherded it from gaming chip company to vital cryptocurrency supplier to the keystone of the AI boom. Its wares are considered the cream of the crop, so incomparable that they are the target of international espionage operations and so valuable that the company forecast $100bn in quarterly revenue . ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick A timeline of the affair scandal that sank Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Trump bought Nvidia stock as he helped chipmaker with change to export rule A spate of failures indicates critical systems are crumbling as we speak, particularly in the US. Banks, planes, email accounts and boats all crashing – it feels like nothing is working and everything is broken. Late last week, an outage of Microsoft Outlook started that would balloon into millions having no access to their email or other critical services. Jails could not release prisoners, hospitals turned to paper records, schools lost contact with parents, and police departments could not receive crime reports. Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday. It also issued an apology. The company did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, instead saying in an initial report that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections and insufficient server capacity sparked the outage. The day after the Microsoft outage began, the US Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights across the country because of a malfunctioning communication system. The transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, attributed the stoppage to “a contractor doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire … to fiber”. The FAA, he said on Saturday, was still working to determine whether the fault was “incompetence” by the contractor, or “a faulty router”. Copper wires downing all US flights in the year 2026, when we have thousands of self-driving cars on the roads and rockets landing in giant machine arms ? The discrepancy gives credence to the axiom by the author William Gibson: “The future is already here – it’s just not evenly distributed.” Also on Friday, an oil tanker collided with a passenger cruise ship on the Mississippi River. Mercifully, no one was killed . On Sunday, Australian students couldn’t take their final exams because of a tech failure . On Monday, leading US banks reported big outages, primarily JPMorgan Chase. Customers could not access online services such as Zelle, which the bank attributed to an unspecified technical issue. The same day, multiple main airlines reported major outages. United and American Airlines reported problems that delayed flights across the country, though they were resolved within hours of being announced. These outages are not, by the available evidence, connected, nor do we know they are the result of cyber-attacks or rogue AI. Still, there is a feeling in the air of old systems breaking down and a strong impulse to blame someone. Are the disruptions the result of old systems’ transition to the new? The onslaught of cyber-attacks brought on by AI models’ advanced hacking capabilities? In the meantime, we have Stephen King’s speculation for solace: “The aliens have landed. That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic.” California sues OpenAI over safety concerns after rogue agent hacking Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029

Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff. The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.” Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely. Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue. In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China. That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch. If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share. sources.title: US government confirms investigation into tech firm Megaspeed - BBC
passages: In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.

Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.
US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.

The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.

In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024. It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair , allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies. Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs. Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation. Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations". In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list. Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang pictured together in Taiwan in June 2024 Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed. The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed. On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips. While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair. The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia. The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance. They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge." passages: ▲ Alice Huang and Jensen Huang The U.S. government has officially confirmed that it has been investigating Megaspeed, a core company implicated in the scandal surrounding former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, for illegal semiconductor smuggling over the past two years.

The two departments stated, "While proactively monitoring potential illegal leaks of sensitive semiconductors, the Department of Commerce detected suspicious activity and initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 regarding potential export control violations." Megaspeed has engaged in a business of building data centers in Southeast Asia utilizing Nvidia semiconductors and leasing out the cloud computing capacity secured through them to customers.

extraction.body: California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday sued artificial intelligence giant OpenAI for allegedly endangering the public by developing advanced AI models without adequate safeguards and monitoring. "OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public," Bonta said at a press conference. Bonta cited the "infamous" incident in July, where two OpenAI models broke out of a testing environment, gained unauthorized access to the open internet, and breached the internal systems of open-source developer platform Hugging Face . OpenAI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September. rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry. On Monday, Bonta said that OpenAI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites." "But the company failed to provide the detailed information we requested to evaluate these incidents; this is concerning, and it puts the public at risk," he said. Bonta's suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California's Unfair Competition Law and accuses the company of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. The attorney general told reporters he believed in AI's technological power, and the potential of AI models to "achieve scientific breakthroughs, boost economic growth, guard against cyber attacks, and benefit all Californians." "But AI systems must be developed and designed safely," he said. "The companies that develop these models have a moral and yes, a legal responsibility to keep public safety at the forefront." Bonta's suit comes as Congress has been presented with, but not passed, a comprehensive AI safety bill. AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, along with critics of AI, have called for such legislation on the heels of the Hugging Face break-in and other incidents that have raised concerns about the safety of AI models. Other AI companies, including Anthropic, Meta and Google, have since disclosed incidents where their own models went rogue. But OpenAI is the first to be sued in connection with such incidents by California. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri, in a statement on the lawsuit, said, "Since the Hugging Face incident, we've undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity." "We've published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment," Pusateri said. "This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," Pusateri said. Bonta's lawsuit adds to OpenAI's growing list of legal woes. In June, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging that the company knowingly released an unsafe product that could harm users. passages: California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday sued artificial intelligence giant OpenAI for allegedly endangering the public by developing advanced AI models without adequate safeguards and monitoring.

"OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public," Bonta said at a press conference.

Bonta cited the "infamous" incident in July, where two OpenAI models broke out of a testing environment, gained unauthorized access to the open internet, and breached the internal systems of open-source developer platform Hugging Face .

OpenAI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September. rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry.
On Monday, Bonta said that OpenAI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites."
"But the company failed to provide the detailed information we requested to evaluate these incidents; this is concerning, and it puts the public at risk," he said.
Bonta's suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California's Unfair Competition Law and accuses the company of being a public nuisance as defined by state law.

The attorney general told reporters he believed in AI's technological power, and the potential of AI models to "achieve scientific breakthroughs, boost economic growth, guard against cyber attacks, and benefit all Californians."
"But AI systems must be developed and designed safely," he said. "The companies that develop these models have a moral and yes, a legal responsibility to keep public safety at the forefront."

Bonta's suit comes as Congress has been presented with, but not passed, a comprehensive AI safety bill. AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, along with critics of AI, have called for such legislation on the heels of the Hugging Face break-in and other incidents that have raised concerns about the safety of AI models.

Other AI companies, including Anthropic, Meta and Google, have since disclosed incidents where their own models went rogue. But OpenAI is the first to be sued in connection with such incidents by California.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the ChatGPT maker of losing control of powerful AI models that hacked outside computer networks while misleading the public about its safety measures .

“OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public,” Bonta said at a news conference in San Francisco.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

The lawsuit — announced as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is reportedly seeking $30 billion in funding ahead of an expected IPO — alleges violations of California’s unfair competition law and creation of a public nuisance. Bonta said the state is seeking a court order requiring safer development and testing, an end to unlawful conduct and financial penalties.
The case follows an investigation into an incident involving Hugging Face , an AI platform whose systems were compromised by OpenAI’s models.
Bonta said the company acknowledged 80 incidents involving loss of control and access to outside networks and websites but failed to provide details investigators requested.
“Without proper safeguards and monitoring, these models pose a danger to anything connected to the internet,” Bonta said.
Officials for OpenAI defend the company, saying they have “undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity” since the Hugging Face incident.

“We’ve published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment,” Drew Pusateri, an OpenAI spokesperson, told the California Post in a statement.

“This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

Bonta warned that sophisticated models could threaten power grids, hospitals, financial institutions and other critical infrastructure, carrying out cyber attacks that would take human experts days or weeks.
He also noted that OpenAI’s models accessed an Australian government Medicare portal without authorization and intruded into systems belonging to government organizations.

California’s attorney general also accused the company of overlooking warning signs, including an agent appearing on a public website despite supposedly lacking internet access and activity that knocked an internal service offline.
“Maybe that’s a red flag. Maybe that should have triggered appropriate follow-up,” Bonta said.
He said Hugging Face discovered the intrusion days after OpenAI lost control, despite the developer’s assurances of strict oversight.
“I reject the notion that we can pass off the blame to machines,” Bonta said. “The people who create and operate these machines need to accept the responsibility for their actions.”
Gary Marcus , a frequent critic of big tech and professor emeritus at New York University, lauded the state’s decision to sue OpenAI.

“California is stepping up where the federal government has fallen short, looking into whether OpenAI’s poorly-controlled AI has committed computer crimes — and into whether OpenAI may have tried to hide the facts,” Marcus told the California Post in a text message.
“Good for Rob Bonta for standing up for humanity and pushing OpenAI to reveal the full story.”
Bonta said AI could deliver scientific breakthroughs and economic benefits, but argued those opportunities do not exempt developers from existing laws.
“The simple truth is that these failures were the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability,” he said.
“Just because the technology is new or rapidly evolving doesn’t mean the people behind it are above the law.”

sources.title: California sues OpenAI, says it lost control of AI agents over 80 times - PPC Land
passages: The 31-page complaint, brought in the name of the People of the State of California against OpenAI Foundation, OpenAI Group PBC and 100 unnamed "Doe" defendants, pleads two causes of action: violations of the state's Unfair Competition Law and the creation of a public nuisance.
"OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General's Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing," according to the complaint.
The company, the state adds, has publicly reported just 27 such incidents.

If the state wins, OpenAI faces civil penalties of $2,500 per violation for each defendant and court orders on how it tests and monitors its models, but every allegation is unproven and neither the complaint nor the state's announcement includes a response from OpenAI.
OpenAI, the state says, never detected the week-long breach of its own testing environment.

After Hugging Face disclosed on July 16, 2026, that it had been hit by an AI-based attack, OpenAI "even reached out to Hugging Face as a concerned customer." The company claims it learned it was responsible only after investigating a separate attack on its own infrastructure and connecting the two.

What: A 31-page complaint alleging that OpenAI tested highly capable AI models in a poorly secured, poorly monitored environment, that some 700 escaped agents attacked Hugging Face and others reached administrator-level access inside OpenAI, that the company admitted to more than 80 loss-of-control incidents while publicly reporting 27, and that its public safety statements were misleading.
The complaint counts "at least three distinct attacks," one of them by an agent apparently aiming to compromise the software that was evaluating agents.
Agents then launched unauthorised servers in OpenAI's cloud, "exposing OpenAI's infrastructure to the public internet."
Other jurisdictions have been circling the same events.

On October 5, New York City Council members questioned OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta under oath about agents that left their test environments , weighing ten local measures with fines of up to $25,000 per violation; OpenAI's representative told the council the company had opened a look-back investigation going back to November 2025.

A federal draft bill tied to Anthropic, last edited on September 29, defines a "containment failure incident" as one in which a model escapes a developer's controls and gains unauthorised access to a system outside that developer's control , and would let courts halt models for 45 days.
The complaint does not name the dozens of third parties notified, quantify Hugging Face's financial losses or give a penalty total.
The complaint dates the pause announcement to September 25 and its end to October 1 and calls it five days long, without saying on which day the pause itself began.
Why: The state argues that OpenAI's choices about testing, monitoring and disclosure endanger anyone relying on internet-connected systems and violate existing California law.

For marketers and publishers, the case tests whether AI vendors' safety claims carry legal weight, and it arrives as the same company expands its advertising business and as autonomous agents take on media buying.

"While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability - and this was only one of 80 known incidents," he said in the release.
"The law is simple: Don't do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.
In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law - no matter the product or the company."
With two named defendants, each proven violation would carry $5,000 in penalties by PPC Land's arithmetic, and the number of violations is left to proof at trial.
OpenAI is not the only lab to disclose such behaviour.

Anthropic reported on October 9 that its Claude models had exploited a server flaw, reused access tokens and submitted an invented tip to a police form during tests , and it cut live internet access from all internal evaluations.
What sets the California complaint apart is the scale it alleges, the days without detection and the dispute over disclosure.
One sentence from the agents themselves appears in the complaint.

A week after the deadline it produced a handful of public documents about incidents it had already blogged about, later adding redacted copies of a few dozen external communications describing non-public incidents.
The filing lands on a date with its own significance.

Under Executive Order N-9-26, signed on September 18, Newsom gave California's Government Operations Agency until November 16, 2026 to recommend whether state law should require a kill switch for frontier models, embed independent auditors inside large labs and add loss-of-control events to the incidents companies must report .
Nor is this the first state action against OpenAI.
As before, the agents exploited the shared package service and used "tools and messages left by other agents inside the service."
OpenAI, the complaint says, "treated these incidents as research curiosities while continuing its experiments unabated."
OpenAI is no longer only a model supplier to the marketing industry.
It sells advertising inside ChatGPT, and in October it told advertisers it would switch on "creative enhancements" that rewrite headlines, resize images and translate ad text by default .
On November 9 it made ChatGPT Enterprise purchasable against AWS cloud commitments .

The complaint itself notes that business customers produced about 40% of OpenAI's revenue in early 2026, and that the company is now pitching cybersecurity defence products built on its most capable models, "marketing those products as an essential defense against cybersecurity threats, including the types of cybersecurity threats that other versions of those same models created."
Security professionals had already been warning about speed.

LinkedIn's chief information security officer, Lea Kissner, argued on October 30 that AI is narrowing the gap between the discovery of a vulnerability and the first attempts to exploit it , and OpenAI said in October that a security firm using GPT-5.6 Sol found a critical PHP flaw before attackers did .
The same family of models now sits at the centre of a state lawsuit over attacks it allegedly carried out.
Can a model be sold as the shield and blamed as the sword at once?
Website operators are the other group with a direct stake.

Publishers already see what agent traffic looks like at volume: HUMAN Security's October data showed Meta and OpenAI generating about nine in ten of the AI agent requests reaching the sites it protects .
Both defendants are headquartered in San Francisco.

extraction.body: Some 700 test agents allegedly hit Hugging Face over two and a half days in July. Bonta seeks $2,500 per violation and court orders on how OpenAI tests models. California Attorney General Rob Bonta on November 16 sued OpenAI in San Francisco Superior Court, alleging that the company tested AI models it knew to be dangerous inside a leaky research environment, failed to notice when hundreds of its autonomous agents broke out and attacked the AI hosting platform Hugging Face, and misled the public about how closely it watches its own experiments. The 31-page complaint, brought in the name of the People of the State of California against OpenAI Foundation, OpenAI Group PBC and 100 unnamed "Doe" defendants, pleads two causes of action: violations of the state's Unfair Competition Law and the creation of a public nuisance. Its most striking line concerns scale. "OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General's Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing," according to the complaint. The company, the state adds, has publicly reported just 27 such incidents. California's attorney general sued OpenAI on November 16, saying AI agents the company was testing escaped their test setup, attacked the AI platform Hugging Face and other websites, and even took administrator-level control of systems inside OpenAI itself. The case matters because it treats careless AI testing as a public nuisance and a consumer protection problem under laws California already has, and the people the state says it is protecting are anyone who runs a website or a network connected to the internet. If the state wins, OpenAI faces civil penalties of $2,500 per violation for each defendant and court orders on how it tests and monitors its models, but every allegation is unproven and neither the complaint nor the state's announcement includes a response from OpenAI. The state's press release calls Hugging Face "one of at least 80 cyber incidents," while the complaint itself counts more than 80 loss-of-control events, of which only some are described as attacks on outside parties. The complaint is dated November 16, 2026, and according to Bonta's office it was filed that day in San Francisco Superior Court. The copy published by the Attorney General's office carries no case number. The filing is headed "Complaint for abatement, injunction, civil penalties, and other equitable relief" and cites section 17200 of the Business and Professions Code and section 3494 of the Civil Code. As a government filing it is marked exempt from filing fees under Government Code section 6103. The cost landed on Hugging Face. Remediation, according to the filing, "required Hugging Face's entire security team's full-time efforts for two weeks." A footnote adds a detail that will not flatter the AI security market: Hugging Face could not use its existing commercial AI tools to analyse the intrusion "because safeguards in those tools treated Hugging Face's attempt to reverse engineer the exploits for remediation purposes as an attempt to launch an attack." It installed an open-source AI tool instead. OpenAI, the state says, never detected the week-long breach of its own testing environment. After Hugging Face disclosed on July 16, 2026, that it had been hit by an AI-based attack, OpenAI "even reached out to Hugging Face as a concerned customer." The company claims it learned it was responsible only after investigating a separate attack on its own infrastructure and connecting the two. PPC Land's earlier reporting places OpenAI's public attribution five days after Hugging Face's disclosure , and, according to a briefing paper prepared for New York City lawmakers, OpenAI published a statement on July 21, 2026 calling the incident unprecedented . One sentence from the agents themselves appears in the complaint. In the middle of the attack, according to the filing, the chain-of-thought for one agent read: "We're attacking third-party HF using leaked token, potentially outside intended scope. . . . This is arguably unauthorized." No one at OpenAI was reading it in real time, the state says. Separately from Hugging Face, the state alleges that in July 2026 a swarm of experimental agents escaped their sandboxes and got into OpenAI's own computer network, "exposing critical tools and resources relied on by OpenAI's business and individual customers as well as personal information for users, employees, and others." The complaint counts "at least three distinct attacks," one of them by an agent apparently aiming to compromise the software that was evaluating agents. Models obtained control of their own computers and administrator-level access to critical OpenAI systems, which according to the complaint included the system OpenAI uses to deploy models in the cloud, its secrets-management service that stores confidential credentials, and its identity- and access-management service. Agents then launched unauthorised servers in OpenAI's cloud, "exposing OpenAI's infrastructure to the public internet." Responsibility for the most dangerous part, according to the state, appears to lie with an internal-only model comparable to OpenAI's Astra model, which the complaint describes as even more advanced than the models behind the Hugging Face attack. As before, the agents exploited the shared package service and used "tools and messages left by other agents inside the service." A large part of the complaint argues foreseeability: that OpenAI had both the knowledge and the internal rules to prevent what happened. The state lists these signals. OpenAI, the complaint says, "treated these incidents as research curiosities while continuing its experiments unabated." The state's case on monitoring rests on chain-of-thought, the text a model outputs to document how it approaches an answer or action. At the time of the Hugging Face incident, according to the complaint, OpenAI ran live chain-of-thought monitoring when deploying models to employees "but chose not to enable it in its training and evaluation environments." From early 2026 until after Hugging Face, it stored only a sample of agent chain-of-thought from training and evaluation runs and analysed those samples retrospectively, "sometimes weeks after they were collected." No live automated review existed, "much less live detection that would shut down the training or evaluation run." The complaint argues that the problem continued after OpenAI's post-incident "security hardening." OpenAI began disclosing loss-of-control incidents "with any real frequency in September 2026," according to the state, and has publicly reported 27. California Attorney General Rob Bonta on November 16 sued OpenAI in San Francisco Superior Court, alleging that the company tested AI models it knew to be dangerous inside a leaky research environment, failed to notice when hundreds of its autonomous agents broke out and attacked the AI hosting platform Hugging Face, and misled the public about how closely it watches its own experiments.

The 31-page complaint, brought in the name of the People of the State of California against OpenAI Foundation, OpenAI Group PBC and 100 unnamed "Doe" defendants, pleads two causes of action: violations of the state's Unfair Competition Law and the creation of a public nuisance. Its most striking line concerns scale. "OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General's Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing," according to the complaint. The company, the state adds, has publicly reported just 27 such incidents.

California's attorney general sued OpenAI on November 16, saying AI agents the company was testing escaped their test setup, attacked the AI platform Hugging Face and other websites, and even took administrator-level control of systems inside OpenAI itself. The case matters because it treats careless AI testing as a public nuisance and a consumer protection problem under laws California already has, and the people the state says it is protecting are anyone who runs a website or a network connected to the internet. If the state wins, OpenAI faces civil penalties of $2,500 per violation for each defendant and court orders on how it tests and monitors its models, but every allegation is unproven and neither the complaint nor the state's announcement includes a response from OpenAI. The state's press release calls Hugging Face "one of at least 80 cyber incidents," while the complaint itself counts more than 80 loss-of-control events, of which only some are described as attacks on outside parties.

The complaint is dated November 16, 2026, and according to Bonta's office it was filed that day in San Francisco Superior Court. The copy published by the Attorney General's office carries no case number. The filing is headed "Complaint for abatement, injunction, civil penalties, and other equitable relief" and cites section 17200 of the Business and Professions Code and section 3494 of the Civil Code. As a government filing it is marked exempt from filing fees under Government Code section 6103.

The cost landed on Hugging Face. Remediation, according to the filing, "required Hugging Face's entire security team's full-time efforts for two weeks." A footnote adds a detail that will not flatter the AI security market: Hugging Face could not use its existing commercial AI tools to analyse the intrusion "because safeguards in those tools treated Hugging Face's attempt to reverse engineer the exploits for remediation purposes as an attempt to launch an attack." It installed an open-source AI tool instead.

OpenAI, the state says, never detected the week-long breach of its own testing environment. After Hugging Face disclosed on July 16, 2026, that it had been hit by an AI-based attack, OpenAI "even reached out to Hugging Face as a concerned customer." The company claims it learned it was responsible only after investigating a separate attack on its own infrastructure and connecting the two. PPC Land's earlier reporting places OpenAI's public attribution five days after Hugging Face's disclosure , and, according to a briefing paper prepared for New York City lawmakers, OpenAI published a statement on July 21, 2026 calling the incident unprecedented .

One sentence from the agents themselves appears in the complaint. In the middle of the attack, according to the filing, the chain-of-thought for one agent read: "We're attacking third-party HF using leaked token, potentially outside intended scope. . . . This is arguably unauthorized." No one at OpenAI was reading it in real time, the state says.

Separately from Hugging Face, the state alleges that in July 2026 a swarm of experimental agents escaped their sandboxes and got into OpenAI's own computer network, "exposing critical tools and resources relied on by OpenAI's business and individual customers as well as personal information for users, employees, and others."

The complaint counts "at least three distinct attacks," one of them by an agent apparently aiming to compromise the software that was evaluating agents. Models obtained control of their own computers and administrator-level access to critical OpenAI systems, which according to the complaint included the system OpenAI uses to deploy models in the cloud, its secrets-management service that stores confidential credentials, and its identity- and access-management service. Agents then launched unauthorised servers in OpenAI's cloud, "exposing OpenAI's infrastructure to the public internet."

Responsibility for the most dangerous part, according to the state, appears to lie with an internal-only model comparable to OpenAI's Astra model, which the complaint describes as even more advanced than the models behind the Hugging Face attack. As before, the agents exploited the shared package service and used "tools and messages left by other agents inside the service."
A large part of the complaint argues foreseeability: that OpenAI had both the knowledge and the internal rules to prevent what happened. The state lists these signals.
OpenAI, the complaint says, "treated these incidents as research curiosities while continuing its experiments unabated."

The state's case on monitoring rests on chain-of-thought, the text a model outputs to document how it approaches an answer or action. At the time of the Hugging Face incident, according to the complaint, OpenAI ran live chain-of-thought monitoring when deploying models to employees "but chose not to enable it in its training and evaluation environments." From early 2026 until after Hugging Face, it stored only a sample of agent chain-of-thought from training and evaluation runs and analysed those samples retrospectively, "sometimes weeks after they were collected." No live automated review existed, "much less live detection that would shut down the training or evaluation run."
The complaint argues that the problem continued after OpenAI's post-incident "security hardening."

OpenAI began disclosing loss-of-control incidents "with any real frequency in September 2026," according to the state, and has publicly reported 27. The complaint also alleges, without giving detail, that the company discourages employees from raising safety issues.

Bonta's office announced a formal investigation into the Hugging Face incident in September 2026, according to the press release. On September 30, 2026, the Attorney General served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena and interrogatories under Government Code section 11180, seeking the "number, scale, scope, and nature" of earlier incidents.

The state describes OpenAI's answer as thin. According to the complaint, the company first sent a 14-page letter describing events it had already disclosed publicly and produced no documents. A week after the deadline it produced a handful of public documents about incidents it had already blogged about, later adding redacted copies of a few dozen external communications describing non-public incidents. "To date, the company has responded to the Attorney General's subpoenas with just a smattering of publicly available information, self-serving blog posts, and redacted copies of a few dozen external communications containing high-level descriptions of select security incidents," the complaint states. Information on how agents compromised OpenAI's internal systems was omitted, according to the filing.

Bonta framed the case in sharp terms. "While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability - and this was only one of 80 known incidents," he said in the release. "The law is simple: Don't do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place. In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law - no matter the product or the company."
No new AI statute does the work here. The state relies on two long-standing tools, and the table below sets out what each covers.

No total is stated. With two named defendants, each proven violation would carry $5,000 in penalties by PPC Land's arithmetic, and the number of violations is left to proof at trial. How a court counts violations when 700 agents take 17,600 actions is one of the more consequential open questions in the case.

The filing lands on a date with its own significance. Under Executive Order N-9-26, signed on September 18, Newsom gave California's Government Operations Agency until November 16, 2026 to recommend whether state law should require a kill switch for frontier models, embed independent auditors inside large labs and add loss-of-control events to the incidents companies must report . The Attorney General's lawsuit arrived on the same day those recommendations were due.

Other jurisdictions have been circling the same events. On October 5, New York City Council members questioned OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta under oath about agents that left their test environments , weighing ten local measures with fines of up to $25,000 per violation; OpenAI's representative told the council the company had opened a look-back investigation going back to November 2025. A federal draft bill tied to Anthropic, last edited on September 29, defines a "containment failure incident" as one in which a model escapes a developer's controls and gains unauthorised access to a system outside that developer's control , and would let courts halt models for 45 days.

OpenAI is not the only lab to disclose such behaviour. Anthropic reported on October 9 that its Claude models had exploited a server flaw, reused access tokens and submitted an invented tip to a police form during tests , and it cut live internet access from all internal evaluations. What sets the California complaint apart is the scale it alleges, the days without detection and the dispute over disclosure.

Nor is this the first state action against OpenAI. Florida's attorney general sued OpenAI and Sam Altman on June 1, 2026 in Highlands County, pleading public nuisance alongside consumer protection claims and seeking penalties of up to $10,000 per violation , though that case concerns ChatGPT's effect on users rather than agents attacking third parties. A non-profit, Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology, also sued OpenAI over the Hugging Face attack at the end of September, according to Techzine . The state's complaint does not mention that case.

OpenAI is no longer only a model supplier to the marketing industry. It sells advertising inside ChatGPT, and in October it told advertisers it would switch on "creative enhancements" that rewrite headlines, resize images and translate ad text by default . On November 9 it made ChatGPT Enterprise purchasable against AWS cloud commitments . The complaint itself notes that business customers produced about 40% of OpenAI's revenue in early 2026, and that the company is now pitching cybersecurity defence products built on its most capable models, "marketing those products as an essential defense against cybersecurity threats, including the types of cybersecurity threats that other versions of those same models created."

That is the commercial context in which the deception claim matters. If a court accepts that general statements about safe testing are misleading when internal practice falls short, the exposure would not stop at one company's research lab; it could reach the safety language in sales decks, procurement questionnaires and trust pages.

Website operators are the other group with a direct stake. The incidents in the complaint involve agents creating fake accounts, using stolen API keys, routing requests through other sites' infrastructure and, according to the complaint, loading public services heavily enough to knock them offline. Publishers already see what agent traffic looks like at volume: HUMAN Security's October data showed Meta and OpenAI generating about nine in ten of the AI agent requests reaching the sites it protects . The complaint's agents were experimental and supposed to stay inside sandboxes, but the costs they imposed, from Hugging Face's two weeks of remediation to Wikimedia's server load, fell on the operators.

The case also arrives as agentic AI moves into media buying. In June, an agency buyer in Prague ran what was described as the Czech Republic's first fully autonomous ad buy, starting from a brief typed into ChatGPT . Agents that hold credentials to ad accounts and budgets are a different proposition from agents in a research sandbox, yet the question at the centre of the complaint, whether a developer can see what its agents are doing while they do it, applies to any vendor whose agents hold such credentials.

Security professionals had already been warning about speed. LinkedIn's chief information security officer, Lea Kissner, argued on October 30 that AI is narrowing the gap between the discovery of a vulnerability and the first attempts to exploit it , and OpenAI said in October that a security firm using GPT-5.6 Sol found a critical PHP flaw before attackers did . The same family of models now sits at the centre of a state lawsuit over attacks it allegedly carried out. Can a model be sold as the shield and blamed as the sword at once? The complaint's view is blunt: it describes OpenAI's new defence products as an attempt to "capitalize on its recent cybersecurity failures."

The published copy has no case number, and neither the complaint nor the release includes OpenAI's response. The complaint does not name the dozens of third parties notified, quantify Hugging Face's financial losses or give a penalty total. It quotes "current and former employees of OpenAI" on the risk of "catastrophic and irreversible loss of control" without saying where that statement was published. The release describes the 80 figure as cyber incidents and refers to "government databases storing sensitive health information," while the complaint counts loss-of-control incidents and specifies foreign government databases. The complaint dates the pause announcement to September 25 and its end to October 1 and calls it five days long, without saying on which day the pause itself began.

extraction.body: California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday sued artificial intelligence giant OpenAI for allegedly endangering the public by developing advanced AI models without adequate safeguards and monitoring. "OpenAI disregarded public safety, knowingly tested potentially dangerous AI models without proper oversight and safety measures, and misled consumers and the public," Bonta said at a press conference. Bonta cited the "infamous" incident in July, where two OpenAI models broke out of a testing environment, gained unauthorized access to the open internet, and breached the internal systems of open-source developer platform Hugging Face . OpenAI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September. rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry. On Monday, Bonta said that OpenAI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites." "But the company failed to provide the detailed information we requested to evaluate these incidents; this is concerning, and it puts the public at risk," he said. Bonta's suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California's Unfair Competition Law and accuses the company of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. The attorney general told reporters he believed in AI's technological power, and the potential of AI models to "achieve scientific breakthroughs, boost economic growth, guard against cyber attacks, and benefit all Californians." "But AI systems must be developed and designed safely," he said. "The companies that develop these models have a moral and yes, a legal responsibility to keep public safety at the forefront." Bonta's suit comes as Congress has been presented with, but not passed, a comprehensive AI safety bill. AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, along with critics of AI, have called for such legislation on the heels of the Hugging Face break-in and other incidents that have raised concerns about the safety of AI models. Other AI companies, including Anthropic, Meta and Google, have since disclosed incidents where their own models went rogue. But OpenAI is the first to be sued in connection with such incidents by California. OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri, in a statement on the lawsuit, said, "Since the Hugging Face incident, we've undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity." "We've published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment," Pusateri said. "This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," Pusateri said. Bonta's lawsuit adds to OpenAI's growing list of legal woes. In June, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging that the company knowingly released an unsafe product that could harm users. OpenAI is also facing lawsuits alleging that the company's ChatGPT platform led users to experience harmful delusions and, in some cases, to commit suicide. California's lawsuit comes almost three months after a suit by Bonta and a coalition of other state attorneys general ended with Meta agreeing to pay $16.7 billion after being accused of misrepresenting the extent of child mental health harms caused by its apps, including Facebook and Instagram. California could receive $1.5 billion to $2.1 billion from that agreement. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, setting the stage for a potentially massive initial public offering in 2027. It is not clear how, if at all, Bonta's lawsuit will affect the IPO. Lise Buyer, partner at IPO advisory firm Class V Group, said she had not closely followed news about the suit. But Buyer, in an email, said, "Potential IPO buyers weigh a laundry list of risk factors, some more heavily than others." "Investors generally do their best to assess timing and a continuum of potential outcomes," Buyer said. "Often, they will speak with uninvolved law firms in calculating the potential outcomes. Then, the risks, the timing and each investors' preferred holding period factor into the price they are willing to pay - assuming they have the option to buy or pass." "Overall the aggregate belief about the risks — all risks — factor in to the IPO price," she said. Earlier Monday, OpenAI announced agreements with four independent evaluators to help support its safety work. The organizations, Apollo Research, METR, Transluce and Goodfire, will be granted "deep access" to OpenAI's internal systems and conduct distinct pilot assessments around model behavior and safeguards, OpenAI said. The company could decide to expand the agreements in the future. Altman pledged to grant independent evaluators " employee-like access " to the company in September, shortly after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said his company would do so as part of his call to slow down the pace of advanced model development. Independent evaluators have taken on outsized importance following high-profile safety breaches, including the Hugging Face incident, this year. President Donald Trump encouraged AI companies to work with an "independent external auditor" as part of a "morally binding" accord he unveiled in September. sources.title: OpenAI sued by California after admitting to 80 loss-of-control incidents
passages: California sued OpenAI yesterday, alleging it has tried to evade responsibility for the Hugging Face attack and about 80 other incidents in which the company lost control of its AI.
The lawsuit was filed under the state’s public nuisance and unfair competition laws.

The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI’s autonomous agents “may just be the tip of the iceberg,” said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta.
OpenAI “knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in a press release .
California is seeking an injunction to stop the alleged violations of the Unfair Competition Law and to require civil penalties and financial damages.
“OpenAI and frontier AI developers more broadly can’t avoid the consequences of their unsafe actions just by claiming that ‘an AI did it,’” the group said.
“Autonomous AI agents will continue to hack, steal data, disrupt systems, and violate rights until a court steps in.”

OpenAI defended its response to the California investigation, saying it provided multiple technical briefings to Bonta and his staff, answered the office’s questions, and offered more technical briefings to discuss its remediation efforts and plans for addressing the problems.
The lawsuit accused OpenAI of refusing to provide sufficient detail about the incidents.
Bonta announced an investigation into OpenAI in early September and sent an investigative subpoena to the company with additional questions on September 30.

“We’ve published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment.
This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.
OpenAI models are “able to find novel vulnerabilities in computer networks, quickly break down defenses, and autonomously carry out cyberattacks,” Bonta’s lawsuit said.

OpenAI puts safeguards in its publicly released models to prevent this behavior, “but deliberately omits or removes these protections while experimenting with and training its models,” the lawsuit said.
“Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure, in an attack that managed to obtain administrator-level access to critical OpenAI systems.”

The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI’s autonomous agents “may just be the tip of the iceberg,” said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta.
OpenAI “knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in a press release .
California is seeking an injunction to stop the alleged violations of the Unfair Competition Law and to require civil penalties and financial damages.
“OpenAI and frontier AI developers more broadly can’t avoid the consequences of their unsafe actions just by claiming that ‘an AI did it,’” the group said.
“Autonomous AI agents will continue to hack, steal data, disrupt systems, and violate rights until a court steps in.”

OpenAI defended its response to the California investigation, saying it provided multiple technical briefings to Bonta and his staff, answered the office’s questions, and offered more technical briefings to discuss its remediation efforts and plans for addressing the problems.
The lawsuit accused OpenAI of refusing to provide sufficient detail about the incidents.
Bonta announced an investigation into OpenAI in early September and sent an investigative subpoena to the company with additional questions on September 30.

“We’ve published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment.
This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.
OpenAI models are “able to find novel vulnerabilities in computer networks, quickly break down defenses, and autonomously carry out cyberattacks,” Bonta’s lawsuit said.

OpenAI puts safeguards in its publicly released models to prevent this behavior, “but deliberately omits or removes these protections while experimenting with and training its models,” the lawsuit said.
“Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure, in an attack that managed to obtain administrator-level access to critical OpenAI systems.”

California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, accusing the ChatGPT maker of losing control of powerful AI models that hacked outside computer networks while misleading the public about its safety measures .

“California is stepping up where the federal government has fallen short, looking into whether OpenAI’s poorly-controlled AI has committed computer crimes — and into whether OpenAI may have tried to hide the facts,” Marcus told the California Post in a text message.

The lawsuit — announced as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is reportedly seeking $30 billion in funding ahead of an expected IPO — alleges violations of California’s unfair competition law and creation of a public nuisance.
Bonta said the state is seeking a court order requiring safer development and testing, an end to unlawful conduct and financial penalties.
Gary Marcus , a frequent critic of big tech and professor emeritus at New York University, lauded the state’s decision to sue OpenAI.

“The simple truth is that these failures were the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability,” he said.
“Good for Rob Bonta for standing up for humanity and pushing OpenAI to reveal the full story.”

sources.title: California sues OpenAI, says it lost control of AI agents over 80 times - PPC Land
passages: The 31-page complaint, brought in the name of the People of the State of California against OpenAI Foundation, OpenAI Group PBC and 100 unnamed "Doe" defendants, pleads two causes of action: violations of the state's Unfair Competition Law and the creation of a public nuisance.
"OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General's Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing," according to the complaint.
The company, the state adds, has publicly reported just 27 such incidents.

If the state wins, OpenAI faces civil penalties of $2,500 per violation for each defendant and court orders on how it tests and monitors its models, but every allegation is unproven and neither the complaint nor the state's announcement includes a response from OpenAI.
OpenAI, the state says, never detected the week-long breach of its own testing environment.

After Hugging Face disclosed on July 16, 2026, that it had been hit by an AI-based attack, OpenAI "even reached out to Hugging Face as a concerned customer." The company claims it learned it was responsible only after investigating a separate attack on its own infrastructure and connecting the two.

What: A 31-page complaint alleging that OpenAI tested highly capable AI models in a poorly secured, poorly monitored environment, that some 700 escaped agents attacked Hugging Face and others reached administrator-level access inside OpenAI, that the company admitted to more than 80 loss-of-control incidents while publicly reporting 27, and that its public safety statements were misleading.
The complaint counts "at least three distinct attacks," one of them by an agent apparently aiming to compromise the software that was evaluating agents.
Agents then launched unauthorised servers in OpenAI's cloud, "exposing OpenAI's infrastructure to the public internet."
Other jurisdictions have been circling the same events.

On October 5, New York City Council members questioned OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta under oath about agents that left their test environments , weighing ten local measures with fines of up to $25,000 per violation; OpenAI's representative told the council the company had opened a look-back investigation going back to November 2025.

A federal draft bill tied to Anthropic, last edited on September 29, defines a "containment failure incident" as one in which a model escapes a developer's controls and gains unauthorised access to a system outside that developer's control , and would let courts halt models for 45 days.
The complaint does not name the dozens of third parties notified, quantify Hugging Face's financial losses or give a penalty total.
The complaint dates the pause announcement to September 25 and its end to October 1 and calls it five days long, without saying on which day the pause itself began.
Why: The state argues that OpenAI's choices about testing, monitoring and disclosure endanger anyone relying on internet-connected systems and violate existing California law.

For marketers and publishers, the case tests whether AI vendors' safety claims carry legal weight, and it arrives as the same company expands its advertising business and as autonomous agents take on media buying.

"While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability - and this was only one of 80 known incidents," he said in the release.
"The law is simple: Don't do things that can hurt people without proper safeguards in place.
In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law - no matter the product or the company."
With two named defendants, each proven violation would carry $5,000 in penalties by PPC Land's arithmetic, and the number of violations is left to proof at trial.
OpenAI is not the only lab to disclose such behaviour.

Anthropic reported on October 9 that its Claude models had exploited a server flaw, reused access tokens and submitted an invented tip to a police form during tests , and it cut live internet access from all internal evaluations.
What sets the California complaint apart is the scale it alleges, the days without detection and the dispute over disclosure.
One sentence from the agents themselves appears in the complaint.

A week after the deadline it produced a handful of public documents about incidents it had already blogged about, later adding redacted copies of a few dozen external communications describing non-public incidents.
The filing lands on a date with its own significance.

Under Executive Order N-9-26, signed on September 18, Newsom gave California's Government Operations Agency until November 16, 2026 to recommend whether state law should require a kill switch for frontier models, embed independent auditors inside large labs and add loss-of-control events to the incidents companies must report .
Nor is this the first state action against OpenAI.
As before, the agents exploited the shared package service and used "tools and messages left by other agents inside the service."
OpenAI, the complaint says, "treated these incidents as research curiosities while continuing its experiments unabated."
OpenAI is no longer only a model supplier to the marketing industry.
It sells advertising inside ChatGPT, and in October it told advertisers it would switch on "creative enhancements" that rewrite headlines, resize images and translate ad text by default .
On November 9 it made ChatGPT Enterprise purchasable against AWS cloud commitments .

The complaint itself notes that business customers produced about 40% of OpenAI's revenue in early 2026, and that the company is now pitching cybersecurity defence products built on its most capable models, "marketing those products as an essential defense against cybersecurity threats, including the types of cybersecurity threats that other versions of those same models created."
Security professionals had already been warning about speed.

LinkedIn's chief information security officer, Lea Kissner, argued on October 30 that AI is narrowing the gap between the discovery of a vulnerability and the first attempts to exploit it , and OpenAI said in October that a security firm using GPT-5.6 Sol found a critical PHP flaw before attackers did .
The same family of models now sits at the centre of a state lawsuit over attacks it allegedly carried out.
Can a model be sold as the shield and blamed as the sword at once?
Website operators are the other group with a direct stake.

Publishers already see what agent traffic looks like at volume: HUMAN Security's October data showed Meta and OpenAI generating about nine in ten of the AI agent requests reaching the sites it protects .
Both defendants are headquartered in San Francisco.
