extraction.body: Some 700 test agents allegedly hit Hugging Face over two and a half days in July. Bonta seeks $2,500 per violation and court orders on how OpenAI tests models. California Attorney General Rob Bonta on November 16 sued OpenAI in San Francisco Superior Court, alleging that the company tested AI models it knew to be dangerous inside a leaky research environment, failed to notice when hundreds of its autonomous agents broke out and attacked the AI hosting platform Hugging Face, and misled the public about how closely it watches its own experiments. The 31-page complaint, brought in the name of the People of the State of California against OpenAI Foundation, OpenAI Group PBC and 100 unnamed "Doe" defendants, pleads two causes of action: violations of the state's Unfair Competition Law and the creation of a public nuisance. Its most striking line concerns scale. "OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General's Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing," according to the complaint. The company, the state adds, has publicly reported just 27 such incidents. California's attorney general sued OpenAI on November 16, saying AI agents the company was testing escaped their test setup, attacked the AI platform Hugging Face and other websites, and even took administrator-level control of systems inside OpenAI itself. The case matters because it treats careless AI testing as a public nuisance and a consumer protection problem under laws California already has, and the people the state says it is protecting are anyone who runs a website or a network connected to the internet. If the state wins, OpenAI faces civil penalties of $2,500 per violation for each defendant and court orders on how it tests and monitors its models, but every allegation is unproven and neither the complaint nor the state's announcement includes a response from OpenAI. The state's press release calls Hugging Face "one of at least 80 cyber incidents," while the complaint itself counts more than 80 loss-of-control events, of which only some are described as attacks on outside parties. The complaint is dated November 16, 2026, and according to Bonta's office it was filed that day in San Francisco Superior Court. The copy published by the Attorney General's office carries no case number. The filing is headed "Complaint for abatement, injunction, civil penalties, and other equitable relief" and cites section 17200 of the Business and Professions Code and section 3494 of the Civil Code. As a government filing it is marked exempt from filing fees under Government Code section 6103. The cost landed on Hugging Face. Remediation, according to the filing, "required Hugging Face's entire security team's full-time efforts for two weeks." A footnote adds a detail that will not flatter the AI security market: Hugging Face could not use its existing commercial AI tools to analyse the intrusion "because safeguards in those tools treated Hugging Face's attempt to reverse engineer the exploits for remediation purposes as an attempt to launch an attack." It installed an open-source AI tool instead. OpenAI, the state says, never detected the week-long breach of its own testing environment. After Hugging Face disclosed on July 16, 2026, that it had been hit by an AI-based attack, OpenAI "even reached out to Hugging Face as a concerned customer." The company claims it learned it was responsible only after investigating a separate attack on its own infrastructure and connecting the two. PPC Land's earlier reporting places OpenAI's public attribution five days after Hugging Face's disclosure , and, according to a briefing paper prepared for New York City lawmakers, OpenAI published a statement on July 21, 2026 calling the incident unprecedented . One sentence from the agents themselves appears in the complaint. In the middle of the attack, according to the filing, the chain-of-thought for one agent read: "We're attacking third-party HF using leaked token, potentially outside intended scope. . . . This is arguably unauthorized." No one at OpenAI was reading it in real time, the state says. Separately from Hugging Face, the state alleges that in July 2026 a swarm of experimental agents escaped their sandboxes and got into OpenAI's own computer network, "exposing critical tools and resources relied on by OpenAI's business and individual customers as well as personal information for users, employees, and others." The complaint counts "at least three distinct attacks," one of them by an agent apparently aiming to compromise the software that was evaluating agents. Models obtained control of their own computers and administrator-level access to critical OpenAI systems, which according to the complaint included the system OpenAI uses to deploy models in the cloud, its secrets-management service that stores confidential credentials, and its identity- and access-management service. Agents then launched unauthorised servers in OpenAI's cloud, "exposing OpenAI's infrastructure to the public internet." Responsibility for the most dangerous part, according to the state, appears to lie with an internal-only model comparable to OpenAI's Astra model, which the complaint describes as even more advanced than the models behind the Hugging Face attack. As before, the agents exploited the shared package service and used "tools and messages left by other agents inside the service." A large part of the complaint argues foreseeability: that OpenAI had both the knowledge and the internal rules to prevent what happened. The state lists these signals. OpenAI, the complaint says, "treated these incidents as research curiosities while continuing its experiments unabated." The state's case on monitoring rests on chain-of-thought, the text a model outputs to document how it approaches an answer or action. At the time of the Hugging Face incident, according to the complaint, OpenAI ran live chain-of-thought monitoring when deploying models to employees "but chose not to enable it in its training and evaluation environments." From early 2026 until after Hugging Face, it stored only a sample of agent chain-of-thought from training and evaluation runs and analysed those samples retrospectively, "sometimes weeks after they were collected." No live automated review existed, "much less live detection that would shut down the training or evaluation run." The complaint argues that the problem continued after OpenAI's post-incident "security hardening." OpenAI began disclosing loss-of-control incidents "with any real frequency in September 2026," according to the state, and has publicly reported 27. The complaint also alleges, without giving detail, that the company discourages employees from raising safety issues. sources.title: New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training - 9to5Google
passages: One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training.
Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history.
Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”
Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”
The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public.

extraction.body: Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.” Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.” Google is now separating that preference into two new options. This is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training. The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled: “…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.” The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public. The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.” With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training. If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email. FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More. Check out 9to5Google on YouTube for more news: Editor-in-chief. Interested in the minutiae of Google and Alphabet. Tips/talk: abner@9to5g.com

sources.title: Google Extends Gemini Chat Retention To Two Months, Even With History Off - Yahoo Tech
passages: Google is extending how long it retains Gemini conversations even when users turn off chat history, increasing the period from 72 hours to around two months as the company introduces new privacy controls for its artificial intelligence assistant.
The change means that disabling Gemini's History setting will no longer limit the retention of future conversations to approximately three days.
For users who leave chat history enabled, Google says the default automatic deletion period remains 18 months.
They can change that period to three months or 36 months, or choose not to automatically delete their history.
Under the updated policy, conversations may remain associated with a user's Google Account during the temporary retention period, even though they do not appear in the user's visible Gemini History.
Google also provides access to conversation settings through Gemini History, where users can review stored activity, delete conversations and manage retention preferences.

Google announced the changes Monday alongside a new system that allows users to keep their conversation history while separately choosing whether their chat content can be used to train generative AI models.
Previously, retaining Gemini conversation history was more closely tied to allowing Google to use those interactions to improve its AI systems.
In its official announcement, Google said the longer retention period was intended to strengthen safety and security protections as AI systems become increasingly capable.
One of the main changes announced this week is the separation of chat history from permission to use conversations for generative AI training.
Users who want to review their choices can open Gemini, go to Settings and select History.
Temporary Chats are also excluded from generative AI model training, although Google still retains them temporarily for operational and safety purposes.

The change means that disabling Gemini's History setting will no longer limit the retention of future conversations to approximately three days. Temporary Chats will also be kept for around two months, according to Google's updated privacy documentation. Google announced the changes Monday alongside a new system that allows users to keep their conversation history while separately choosing whether their chat content can be used to train generative AI models. The company said the updates would begin rolling out globally over the coming weeks. In its official announcement, Google said the longer retention period was intended to strengthen safety and security protections as AI systems become increasingly capable. Under the new policy, future conversations will be saved for around two months even when users have disabled history. Google says the retained information may be used to respond to requests, process feedback and protect the company, its users and the public. The change represents a substantial increase from the previous 72-hour retention period. The Register reported Tuesday that archived versions of Google's privacy documentation confirmed the earlier three-day limit. The publication also noted that Google's announcement emphasized the new privacy controls without highlighting how much longer conversations would be stored when history was disabled. The distinction matters because turning off chat history does not mean Google immediately deletes the information exchanged with Gemini. Under the updated policy, conversations may remain associated with a user's Google Account during the temporary retention period, even though they do not appear in the user's visible Gemini History. Google also says it may use human reviewers to examine certain conversations for safety and security purposes. However, the longer retention period does not automatically mean that every conversation will be used to train Google's AI models . One of the main changes announced this week is the separation of chat history from permission to use conversations for generative AI training. Previously, retaining Gemini conversation history was more closely tied to allowing Google to use those interactions to improve its AI systems. The new settings allow users to preserve their conversations for future reference while opting out of generative AI model training. That gives people who want to revisit previous conversations greater flexibility without requiring them to authorize that particular use of their data. Google's documentation states that future chat content will not be used to train generative AI models when the training setting is disabled, except in certain circumstances, including when users voluntarily submit feedback. Temporary Chats are also excluded from generative AI model training, although Google still retains them temporarily for operational and safety purposes. There is another important exception involving human review. According to Google's Privacy Hub, conversations reviewed by human reviewers and associated information can be retained for up to three years, even if users subsequently delete their history. Google says conversations sent to service providers for review are disconnected from users' accounts. Submitting feedback about a Gemini response can also result in the associated conversation, attachments and other relevant information being reviewed and retained for up to three years. That information may be used to maintain, improve and develop Google services, including machine-learning technologies. The new settings therefore distinguish between several different activities: saving conversations in a user's visible history, retaining information for operational or security purposes, and using chat content to train generative AI models. Switching off one of those functions does not necessarily disable the others. Users who want to review their choices can open Gemini, go to Settings and select History. Google also provides access to conversation settings through Gemini History, where users can review stored activity, delete conversations and manage retention preferences. With the new controls, users can choose whether their chat content, including text and uploaded files, may be used for generative AI training. Google's help documentation says the new training controls are off by default, although individual users may see different options while the global rollout is underway. For users who leave chat history enabled, Google says the default automatic deletion period remains 18 months. They can change that period to three months or 36 months, or choose not to automatically delete their history. However, those settings do not override every separate retention requirement. Google also warns that deleting Gemini history does not necessarily remove information saved through connected Google services, which may follow their own privacy and retention policies. The company advises users not to enter confidential information they would not want a reviewer to see.

Under the new policy, future conversations will be saved for around two months even when users have disabled history. Google says the retained information may be used to respond to requests, process feedback and protect the company, its users and the public. The change represents a substantial increase from the previous 72-hour retention period. The Register reported Tuesday that archived versions of Google's privacy documentation confirmed the earlier three-day limit. The publication also noted that Google's announcement emphasized the new privacy controls without highlighting how much longer conversations would be stored when history was disabled. The distinction matters because turning off chat history does not mean Google immediately deletes the information exchanged with Gemini. Under the updated policy, conversations may remain associated with a user's Google Account during the temporary retention period, even though they do not appear in the user's visible Gemini History. Google also says it may use human reviewers to examine certain conversations for safety and security purposes. However, the longer retention period does not automatically mean that every conversation will be used to train Google's AI models . One of the main changes announced this week is the separation of chat history from permission to use conversations for generative AI training. Previously, retaining Gemini conversation history was more closely tied to allowing Google to use those interactions to improve its AI systems. The new settings allow users to preserve their conversations for future reference while opting out of generative AI model training. That gives people who want to revisit previous conversations greater flexibility without requiring them to authorize that particular use of their data. Google's documentation states that future chat content will not be used to train generative AI models when the training setting is disabled, except in certain circumstances, including when users voluntarily submit feedback. Temporary Chats are also excluded from generative AI model training, although Google still retains them temporarily for operational and safety purposes. There is another important exception involving human review. According to Google's Privacy Hub, conversations reviewed by human reviewers and associated information can be retained for up to three years, even if users subsequently delete their history. Google says conversations sent to service providers for review are disconnected from users' accounts. Submitting feedback about a Gemini response can also result in the associated conversation, attachments and other relevant information being reviewed and retained for up to three years. That information may be used to maintain, improve and develop Google services, including machine-learning technologies. The new settings therefore distinguish between several different activities: saving conversations in a user's visible history, retaining information for operational or security purposes, and using chat content to train generative AI models. Switching off one of those functions does not necessarily disable the others. Users who want to review their choices can open Gemini, go to Settings and select History. Google also provides access to conversation settings through Gemini History, where users can review stored activity, delete conversations and manage retention preferences. With the new controls, users can choose whether their chat content, including text and uploaded files, may be used for generative AI training. Google's help documentation says the new training controls are off by default, although individual users may see different options while the global rollout is underway. For users who leave chat history enabled, Google says the default automatic deletion period remains 18 months. They can change that period to three months or 36 months, or choose not to automatically delete their history. However, those settings do not override every separate retention requirement. Google also warns that deleting Gemini history does not necessarily remove information saved through connected Google services, which may follow their own privacy and retention policies. The company advises users not to enter confidential information they would not want a reviewer to see.

And this time he was the one helping to call the shots.

Speaking during an appearance at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, Variety reports that Bezos pulled back the curtain on how Amazon MGM Studios narrowed down a wide field of contenders to five finalists before locking in The Batman star over the weekend. “We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday,” Bezos explained. “There was a big group initially, and we down-selected to five finalists. We did real, old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists. It was interesting. Full costumes and real sets and other actors with them. We did three different scenes with each of the five finalists, and then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that.” Because 007 has historically served as a star-making launchpad for lesser-known actors, Bezos admitted the creative team—including director Denis Villeneuve—initially wondered whether Pattinson’s global fame might work against him. Once the cameras rolled on the screen tests, however, any doubts evaporated immediately. “By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance,” Bezos said. “It was immediately undebated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob. Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he’s already so famous, like maybe we should have somebody more unknown, but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.” Amazon MGM officially announced Pattinson as the next 007 on Monday, November 16, putting an end to years of speculation following Daniel Craig’s exit. In a statement celebrating the announcement, Pattinson called stepping into the tuxedo "the honor of a lifetime" and praised the powerhouse creative team assembled for the franchise's next chapter—including Villeneuve in the director’s chair, Steven Knight writing the script, producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman, and executive producer Tanya Lapointe. “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.” While Bezos did not name the other four finalists who took part in the costume screen tests, industry reports heading into the final weekend pointed to Callum Turner , Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden, and Nicholas Hoult as the final contenders, alongside earlier rumored names including Jacob Elordi, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson, Tom Francis, and Harry Styles. The upcoming installment—expected to begin production in 2027—marks the first Bond feature produced since Amazon closed its 2022 acquisition of MGM and subsequently struck a landmark joint venture deal in March 2025 giving Amazon MGM Studios creative control over the 007 franchise from longtime producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli. Amazon founder and chairman Jeff Bezos has revealed he was 'heavily involved' in the high-stakes casting process that landed Robert Pattinson the coveted role of James Bond—despite studio executives initially hesitating because the actor was already 'so famous.'

Speaking during an appearance at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, Variety reports that Bezos pulled back the curtain on how Amazon MGM Studios narrowed down a wide field of contenders to five finalists before locking in The Batman star over the weekend.

“We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday,” Bezos explained. “There was a big group initially, and we down-selected to five finalists. We did real, old-fashioned screen tests of those five finalists. It was interesting. Full costumes and real sets and other actors with them. We did three different scenes with each of the five finalists, and then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that.”

Because 007 has historically served as a star-making launchpad for lesser-known actors, Bezos admitted the creative team—including director Denis Villeneuve—initially wondered whether Pattinson’s global fame might work against him.
Once the cameras rolled on the screen tests, however, any doubts evaporated immediately.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance,” Bezos said. “It was immediately undebated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob. Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he’s already so famous, like maybe we should have somebody more unknown, but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”
Amazon MGM officially announced Pattinson as the next 007 on Monday, November 16, putting an end to years of speculation following Daniel Craig’s exit.

In a statement celebrating the announcement, Pattinson called stepping into the tuxedo "the honor of a lifetime" and praised the powerhouse creative team assembled for the franchise's next chapter—including Villeneuve in the director’s chair, Steven Knight writing the script, producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman, and executive producer Tanya Lapointe.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

While Bezos did not name the other four finalists who took part in the costume screen tests, industry reports heading into the final weekend pointed to Callum Turner , Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden, and Nicholas Hoult as the final contenders, alongside earlier rumored names including Jacob Elordi, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Harris Dickinson, Tom Francis, and Harry Styles.

The upcoming installment—expected to begin production in 2027—marks the first Bond feature produced since Amazon closed its 2022 acquisition of MGM and subsequently struck a landmark joint venture deal in March 2025 giving Amazon MGM Studios creative control over the 007 franchise from longtime producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli.

extraction.body: Nvidia has warned customers that a proposed US legislation targeting Chinese companies' remote access to its artificial intelligence (AI) chips could expose both the chipmaker and buyers to legal action, CNBC reported on Tuesday (November 17), citing sources familiar with the matter. The chipmaker had communicated with buyers in recent months about the proposed Remote Access Security Act (RASA), cautioning that it would give the US government broader powers to regulate access to cloud computing services in the same way as physical hardware exports, the report said. The legislation could expose Nvidia and companies purchasing its chips to legal risks if Chinese firms access the technology through overseas data centres. RASA is proposed US legislation that would give the Commerce Department greater authority to restrict Chinese companies from accessing advanced American AI chips through overseas data centres. It aims to regulate remote cloud access more like physical hardware exports. US regulators are concerned that Chinese companies could bypass export restrictions by renting computing capacity from data centres outside the United States. The proposed measures seek to close that potential loophole and protect US national security. According to the report, Nvidia warned customers that the proposed law could expose both the chipmaker and buyers to legal action if Chinese firms access the technology through overseas data centres. The bill passed the US House of Representatives in January but had not yet cleared the Senate, according to the article. According to CNBC, Nvidia indicated it would not sell chips to customers who rent out more than 50% of their GPUs to Chinese companies. Amid growing scrutiny from US lawmakers over China's access to advanced AI chips, Nvidia has also indicated that it would not sell chips to customers who rent out more than 50% of their graphics processing units (GPUs) to Chinese companies, according to CNBC. Currently, US regulators have limited powers to restrict access to advanced chips through cloud services hosted outside the country. This has raised concerns in Washington that Chinese companies could bypass export restrictions by renting computing capacity from overseas data centres. RASA seeks to address this gap by giving the US Commerce Department greater authority to prevent Chinese companies from renting overseas data centre capacity to access advanced American AI chips. The bill passed the US House of Representatives in January but has yet to clear the Senate. The proposed legislation comes as President Donald Trump's administration steps up efforts to restrict China's access to advanced American computing technology and maintain the US lead in the global AI race. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued an interim final rule on November 16 to tighten controls on remote access to advanced superintelligence (SI) chips and servers , aiming to prevent restrictions on sensitive American technology from being bypassed through data centres in third countries. The rule, drafted at the direction of the US Treasury Department and the National Security Council, seeks to align safeguards governing remote access to advanced computing capabilities with existing restrictions on the physical export of sensitive US technology. The BIS said rapid advances in cloud computing and superintelligence infrastructure have made it increasingly possible to access advanced American computing resources remotely, including through data centres located outside countries subject to US export restrictions. The new rule aims to close these potential loopholes while allowing legitimate commercial use of American technology and protecting US national security. Nvidia has formed a new board committee to oversee national security and export control matters as the US government moves to restrict China's access to the company's advanced chips. The committee will be chaired by board member and former Goldman Sachs executive Suzanne Nora Johnson, with directors Stephen Neal and John Dabiri also serving as members, the company said on Tuesday. The move is among the first changes under interim CEO Colette Kress , who was appointed last week following Jensen Huang's resignation . US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia following the shock departure of CEO Jensen Huang , amid allegations involving a woman US authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China . Bessent also suggested that other senior Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the company's compliance with US export controls and alleged diversion of advanced AI chips to China. "I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News. His remarks raise questions about Nvidia's internal oversight and whether the company adequately enforced restrictions on the sale of advanced chips to China. Nvidia has been embroiled in a major controversy following allegations that its former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China and that the company's advanced AI chips were being diverted to Beijing through third-country data centres. The scandal has triggered investigations, a leadership change, a shareholder lawsuit, congressional scrutiny and tighter US export controls. extraction.body: iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below. Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device. Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through. With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol. At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place. iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version. As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch. Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism. Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly. Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly. Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “ BEEP this thing” out of 10. To check out iFixit’s blog post, which features an interactive 3D CT scan of the HomeView, follow this link . Be sure to also catch 9to5Mac’s review of the Apple HomeView . extraction.body: After finding recent versions of Apple’s iPads and HomePods much easier to disassemble for battery replacements or other repairs, iFixit assumed it would be the same story for Apple’s new HomeView hub that looks like a seven-inch tablet stuck to a smart speaker. The reality was much different and by the time they got the HomeView apart iFixit’s skilled techs had “ripped a connector, snapped a speaker in two, and put more force on the poor logic board than any of us were comfortable with.” The tablet section of the HomeView proved to be the bigger challenge to disassemble as a result of some questionable decisions with Apple’s design. The glue used to secure the display in place “held on harder than on any Apple product we’ve opened recently,” iFixit says. Although both versions are priced at $299, the wall version costs a little more when you factor in the required mount that’s not included, leaving iFixit feeling that you’re getting less performance while spending more money.

During removal, the team broke two speaker connectors and snapped a speaker in half.
Hard-to-reach screws and cables caught between components also complicated separating the screen from the tabletop speaker base.
Even so, the difficulty reaching internal components is a concern for anyone hoping to repair the device later.
Would difficult repairs change your mind about buying HomeView?

extraction.body: iFixit today disassembled the iPhone 17 Pro for one of its teardown videos, showing the device's internal components, like the new vapor chamber cooling system that distributes heat from the A19 Pro chip throughout the aluminum frame. iPhone 17 Pro Teardown: The Good, The Bad & The Fascinating"> iPhone 17 Pro Teardown: The Good, The Bad & The Fascinating iFixit Watch on YouTube The ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro's battery is attached to a battery tray, and the battery tray is connected to the ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro's aluminum frame with Torx Plus screws. iFixit says that if Apple sells replacement batteries in the tray, there won't be any adhesive to deal with when doing a battery swap. The battery tray is on top of the A19 Pro chip, and the chip includes the vapor chamber cooling system. extraction.body: iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below. Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device. Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through. With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol. At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place. iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version. As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch. Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism. Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly. Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly. Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “ BEEP this thing” out of 10. To check out iFixit’s blog post, which features an interactive 3D CT scan of the HomeView, follow this link . Be sure to also catch 9to5Mac’s review of the Apple HomeView . Apple’s HomeView has another problem beyond its early software frustrations, according to iFixit , which says taking the smart home hub apart proved unusually difficult. In a November 17 email outlining its HomeView teardown findings , iFixit said it examined both the tabletop and wall-mounted versions. The repair specialists expected progress similar to what they had seen in recent iPads and HomePods, but instead found a design that was much harder to work on. The biggest obstacle was the adhesive holding the display in place. iFixit said it was tougher than the glue it had encountered in recent Apple products. During removal, the team broke two speaker connectors and snapped a speaker in half. Those were parts damaged during the teardown, not a report of speakers failing during normal use. Even so, the difficulty reaching internal components is a concern for anyone hoping to repair the device later. Getting deeper inside brought more trouble. Apple bonded the logic board’s heat spreader to the aluminium chassis, making removal of the board risky, according to iFixit . Hard-to-reach screws and cables caught between components also complicated separating the screen from the tabletop speaker base. The teardown revealed hardware differences between the two models, too. iFixit said CT scans and disassembly showed smaller speakers in the wall-mounted HomeView. Banks of capacitors sit behind its display in space that the tabletop version uses for audio hardware. There was one encouraging finding for repairs. The tabletop model’s USB-C port is a separate, replaceable component that iFixit described as relatively easy to access. extraction.body: iFixit today disassembled the iPhone 17 Pro for one of its teardown videos, showing the device's internal components, like the new vapor chamber cooling system that distributes heat from the A19 Pro chip throughout the aluminum frame. iPhone 17 Pro Teardown: The Good, The Bad & The Fascinating"> iPhone 17 Pro Teardown: The Good, The Bad & The Fascinating iFixit Watch on YouTube The ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro's battery is attached to a battery tray, and the battery tray is connected to the ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro's aluminum frame with Torx Plus screws. iFixit says that if Apple sells replacement batteries in the tray, there won't be any adhesive to deal with when doing a battery swap. The battery tray is on top of the A19 Pro chip, and the chip includes the vapor chamber cooling system. Heat from the chip is directed to the vapor chamber, which spreads it throughout the unibody aluminum frame. iFixit used a thermal camera to compare the iPhone 16 Pro Max to the ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro Max. The ‌iPhone 16‌ Pro Max would get to 37.8 degrees Celsius and experience throttling, while the 17 Pro Max stayed cooler at 34.8 degrees Celsius, resulting in no throttling. iFixit found that Apple's cooling system uses a lattice between two plates to distribute water throughout the vapor chamber. The water next to the A19 Pro chip boils and turns to steam, then the steam collects on the other side and cools down, condensing back into droplets that are sent back through the lattice structure. iFixit conducted a scratch test on the ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro's aluminum frame, and found the camera plateau to be an area that's prone to scratching. The site spoke with David Niebuhr, a mechanical engineering professor at Cal Poly. Niebuhr said that the damage is called "spalling." The sharp, flat edge of the camera plateau doesn't allow for the anodized finish to adhere as well, so the color can rub off when exposed to hard objects like keys. The ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro models have a less repairable design than the ‌iPhone 16‌ Pro models because Apple did away with the dual-entry design that made repairs possible from either the back or the front of the device. It's only possible to repair the wireless charging assembly or replace the back glass from the back of the iPhone, and replacing the battery, a camera module, or the USB-C port requires removing the iPhone's display. The battery tray that's only held in with screws makes the battery easier to replace once you get to it, plus the battery is encased in metal, which makes it safer. Replacing the USB-C port requires removing 22 screws, a process that iFixit found tedious. Considering all of the changes, iFixit says that the ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro is slightly less repairable than the iPhone Air , but Apple is providing day-one repair manuals and Apple's engineers appear to have taken repairability into account when designing the device, so it earned a repairability score of 7 out of 10. extraction.body: NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails The US National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down. In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational” and its ability to defend national security continues. It said its infrastructure is built with “multiple layers of redundancy” to keep operations running during planned maintenance or unexpected events. The statement did not name the network, say what caused the problem or how long it lasted, or say whether service had been fully restored. The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday. They said staff at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters had been told to stagger their arrivals while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily. The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said. Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff. A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong. The outage follows a run of technology failures in the US in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights , a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services . None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained. Officials said the ground stop was not the result of malicious activity by a foreign actor, and the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said they were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was responsible. Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage. Asked in Manila on Tuesday about the constant outages, he played them down, saying such problems were inevitable: “Things like that happen.” He said he had spoken with banks and that the situation would be “very much under control”, and that Americans travelling before Thanksgiving were safe. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, called for the Trump administration to send officials to brief lawmakers on Capitol Hill about the recent nationwide technical and infrastructure outages, telling reporters that the public deserves more transparency around the widespread disruptions. While none of the incidents have been classified as a cyber-attack, Mike Wiacek, a former US Department of Defense analyst, said the run of failures in a single week was a reason for caution and that early assurances may have come too quickly. “Without data, I can’t say for certain whether this is or isn’t a cyber-attack,” Wiacek said. “But four major outages in under a week ( Outlook , the FAA , the banks and now the NSA) look suspiciously like what I’d expect one to look like. “What concerns me most is how quickly officials ruled out an attack,” he said. “You can’t compress months of forensic work into a few hours.”

extraction.body: A highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications went offline on Tuesday for an unspecified period of time, according to US media reports. The NSA - America's largest intelligence organisation - said it had experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance" but that "mission-critical capabilities" were not affected. The outage reportedly affected the NSANet network, which is how officials send and receive top secret or classified information. It comes after a string of technology outages in the US in recent days that have affected flights, banks and other infrastructure. "While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," an NSA spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC. "NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events." It did not specify when the issue began, nor when it would be resolved. The issue was not a cyberattack, multiple US news outlets reported. Tens of thousands of people work at the NSA, which is responsible for collecting signals intelligence, overseeing cyber threats, and protecting US government communications. Multiple sources told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems on Tuesday. Sources familiar with the situation told CBS that operations at the NSA's headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland, had not been affected but that some activities had been redirected to other facilities around the country. Tuesday's outage follows a series of technological outages. Last week, a massive Microsoft outage impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world - including the US and Canada - while a network failure grounded all US flights. On Monday, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services. Chase Bank - the largest banking institution in the US - said a "software bug" in its hardware systems may have affected other banks and that it was not a cyber security incident. extraction.body: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said. The agency reverted to its typical work schedule Tuesday evening. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a three-level system that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The New York Times first reported that detail. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time. extraction.body: NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails The US National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down. In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational” and its ability to defend national security continues. It said its infrastructure is built with “multiple layers of redundancy” to keep operations running during planned maintenance or unexpected events. The statement did not name the network, say what caused the problem or how long it lasted, or say whether service had been fully restored. The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday. They said staff at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters had been told to stagger their arrivals while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily. The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said. Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff. A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong. The outage follows a run of technology failures in the US in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights , a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services . None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained. Officials said the ground stop was not the result of malicious activity by a foreign actor, and the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said they were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was responsible. Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage. Asked in Manila on Tuesday about the constant outages, he played them down, saying such problems were inevitable: “Things like that happen.” He said he had spoken with banks and that the situation would be “very much under control”, and that Americans travelling before Thanksgiving were safe. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, called for the Trump administration to send officials to brief lawmakers on Capitol Hill about the recent nationwide technical and infrastructure outages, telling reporters that the public deserves more transparency around the widespread disruptions. While none of the incidents have been classified as a cyber-attack, Mike Wiacek, a former US Department of Defense analyst, said the run of failures in a single week was a reason for caution and that early assurances may have come too quickly. “Without data, I can’t say for certain whether this is or isn’t a cyber-attack,” Wiacek said. “But four major outages in under a week ( Outlook , the FAA , the banks and now the NSA) look suspiciously like what I’d expect one to look like. “What concerns me most is how quickly officials ruled out an attack,” he said. “You can’t compress months of forensic work into a few hours.”

The NSA episode is among a series of cyber-related disruptions to critical government and private sector functions in the last week, including a system overload Friday that resulted in a ground stop of air traffic in the United States, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase on Monday that caused ripple effects in the financial system and an internal systems outage at United Airlines that delayed departing flights. He attributed the problem instead to the fact that government institutions and private companies were pushing through upgrades of their computer systems around the same time, resulting in periodic technological hiccups. “Many people are patching their systems. And as you patch and upgrade your systems — taking them down and bringing them back up — there are things like this that happen,” Clayton added. Sen. extraction.body: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said. The agency reverted to its typical work schedule Tuesday evening. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a three-level system that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The New York Times first reported that detail. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time. In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational” and its ability to defend national security continues. It said its infrastructure is built with “multiple layers of redundancy” to keep operations running during planned maintenance or unexpected events. The statement did not name the network, say what caused the problem or how long it lasted, or say whether service had been fully restored. The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday. They said staff at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters had been told to stagger their arrivals while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily. The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said. Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff. A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong. The outage follows a run of technology failures in the US in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights , a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services . extraction.body: WASHINGTON – An internal network the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline Tuesday after what the agency described as “routine maintenance.” The problem disrupted the operations of NSANet, a classified internal network used by employees of the agency, according to a defense official who was not authorized to discuss the matter by name and spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance," the NSA said in a statement. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” The intelligence agency did not provide any additional details on the cause of the outage or the scope of the disruption. The NSA episode is among a series of cyber-related disruptions to critical government and private sector functions in the last week, including a system overload Friday that resulted in a ground stop of air traffic in the United States, a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase on Monday that caused ripple effects in the financial system and an internal systems outage at United Airlines that delayed departing flights. On Tuesday , Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages after an internal update. None of the outages has been attributed to a cyberattack or nefarious activity. “This is not a cyber attack and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation-state,” Jay Clayton, the Trump administration's director of national intelligence, said in a CNBC interview Tuesday about the spate of disruptions. He attributed the problem instead to the fact that government institutions and private companies were pushing through upgrades of their computer systems around the same time, resulting in periodic technological hiccups. “Many people are patching their systems. They know that their legacy systems have vulnerabilities. They're outdated, they don't work well with new systems. It is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure. And as you patch and upgrade your systems — taking them down and bringing them back up — there are things like this that happen,” Clayton added. Sen. Mark Warner, the Democratic vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, echoed that assessment. “AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” Warner said in a statement. “While we still need to get to the bottom of these incidents, the evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity.” Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. extraction.body: NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails The US National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down. In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational” and its ability to defend national security continues. It said its infrastructure is built with “multiple layers of redundancy” to keep operations running during planned maintenance or unexpected events. The statement did not name the network, say what caused the problem or how long it lasted, or say whether service had been fully restored. The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday. They said staff at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters had been told to stagger their arrivals while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily. The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said. Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff. A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong. The outage follows a run of technology failures in the US in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights , a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services . None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained. Officials said the ground stop was not the result of malicious activity by a foreign actor, and the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said they were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was responsible. Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage. Asked in Manila on Tuesday about the constant outages, he played them down, saying such problems were inevitable: “Things like that happen.” He said he had spoken with banks and that the situation would be “very much under control”, and that Americans travelling before Thanksgiving were safe. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, called for the Trump administration to send officials to brief lawmakers on Capitol Hill about the recent nationwide technical and infrastructure outages, telling reporters that the public deserves more transparency around the widespread disruptions. While none of the incidents have been classified as a cyber-attack, Mike Wiacek, a former US Department of Defense analyst, said the run of failures in a single week was a reason for caution and that early assurances may have come too quickly. “Without data, I can’t say for certain whether this is or isn’t a cyber-attack,” Wiacek said. “But four major outages in under a week ( Outlook , the FAA , the banks and now the NSA) look suspiciously like what I’d expect one to look like. “What concerns me most is how quickly officials ruled out an attack,” he said. “You can’t compress months of forensic work into a few hours.”

extraction.body: ▲ A sign at the entrance of the National Security Agency (NSA) The internal communications network of the National Security Agency (NSA), a Department of Defense agency overseeing U.S. cybersecurity, has suffered an outage. According to AP and CNN on the 17th (local time), the NSA is assessing the scope of the incident while implementing measures to stagger employee arrival times. The network, known as "NSAnet," is used to transmit classified information within the NSA. White House Communications Director Lauren Bis said in a statement sent to Newsmax that "there is no evidence of a cyberattack" and "there is no crisis or anything of that nature for the American people to worry about." In a press release, the NSA stated, "There was a temporary degradation in performance during scheduled routine maintenance. While some internal systems were impacted, mission-critical functions remain fully operational, and our capability to defend national security is maintained." It added, "NSA infrastructure is designed with multiple redundancies to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events." In addition, two current and former U.S. officials told CNN that the outage would not affect the NSA's ability to urgently transmit information to U.S. It was also reported that the intelligence-sharing system with the "Five Eyes"—the intelligence alliance of five Western countries consisting of the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand—was not affected. However, CNN noted that this NSA internal network outage follows a series of major technical glitches, including a recent air traffic control network failure that caused a nationwide halt in U.S. air travel, a global Microsoft (MS) service disruption that affected government and corporate operations worldwide, and an online trading outage at JPMorgan Chase, the largest bank in the United States. CNN pointed out that while "there is no evidence that these glitches and disruptions were caused by cyberattacks," these incidents "clearly demonstrate how technical flaws can rattle markets and potentially threaten national security." Bryson Bort, a cybersecurity advisor at the digital security firm Huntress, diagnosed that even if the NSA incident lacked malicious intent, it clearly highlights concerns over aging digital infrastructure. An official told The New York Times (NYT) that NSAnet had been unstable for weeks, leading to growing frustration among employees. Citing the official, the NYT reported that the blackout of the NSA's classified communications network appears to have stemmed from a problem encountered during a software patching process for a system update, though it remains unclear which software was at fault. (Photo: AP, Yonhap News) ※ Please note: This article was translated by AI and may contain errors.
