extraction.body: NSA issues ‘code yellow’ as NSANet, used by staff to share classified material, including top-secret intelligence, fails The US National Security Agency said on Tuesday that it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down. In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but that “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational” and its ability to defend national security continues. It said its infrastructure is built with “multiple layers of redundancy” to keep operations running during planned maintenance or unexpected events. The statement did not name the network, say what caused the problem or how long it lasted, or say whether service had been fully restored. The New York Times and CNN had earlier reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that NSANet, the network the agency uses to send and receive classified information including top-secret material, was offline on Tuesday. They said staff at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters had been told to stagger their arrivals while it assessed the problem. The Wall Street Journal also reported the outage, citing one person familiar with the situation, who said it stemmed from a software update to patch the system and that it would only be down temporarily. The Times reported that a recorded message on an employee information line described a “code yellow”, the second-highest level in a three-tier alert system, for the day shift. Non-emergency staff were told not to come in before noon, while emergency personnel were to report as scheduled, the paper said. Both CNN and the Times, citing people familiar with the matter, said there was no sign so far that the outage was caused by a cyber-attack or other malicious activity. The Times, citing one person, reported that the network had been unstable for weeks, and had been a cause of frustration among staff. A former senior NSA cybersecurity official, who has no knowledge of the incident beyond public reports, speculated that several software patches may have been applied at once and something had gone wrong. The outage follows a run of technology failures in the US in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights , a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services . None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained. Officials said the ground stop was not the result of malicious activity by a foreign actor, and the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said they were investigating whether contractor error or a faulty router was responsible. Trump has not commented directly on the NSA outage. Asked in Manila on Tuesday about the constant outages, he played them down, saying such problems were inevitable: “Things like that happen.” He said he had spoken with banks and that the situation would be “very much under control”, and that Americans travelling before Thanksgiving were safe. Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, called for the Trump administration to send officials to brief lawmakers on Capitol Hill about the recent nationwide technical and infrastructure outages, telling reporters that the public deserves more transparency around the widespread disruptions. While none of the incidents have been classified as a cyber-attack, Mike Wiacek, a former US Department of Defense analyst, said the run of failures in a single week was a reason for caution and that early assurances may have come too quickly. “Without data, I can’t say for certain whether this is or isn’t a cyber-attack,” Wiacek said. “But four major outages in under a week ( Outlook , the FAA , the banks and now the NSA) look suspiciously like what I’d expect one to look like. “What concerns me most is how quickly officials ruled out an attack,” he said. “You can’t compress months of forensic work into a few hours.”

extraction.body: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said. The agency reverted to its typical work schedule Tuesday evening. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. The NSA itself urged organizations to apply software patches. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a three-level system that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The New York Times first reported that detail. It was not immediately clear whether the outage was resolved. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time. This story has been updated with additional information. Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP).

coreStoryFacts.text: Apple services are having a rough Tuesday. iCloud, the App Store, and other services are experiencing an apparent outage, with users reporting connection failures and trouble signing in.
Developers have separately reported trouble accessing App Store Connect .
Apple retail stores and corporate offices are also reportedly experiencing outages.
Apple: “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning.
We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible." Company says this wasn’t a cyberattack.
Developer-focused services are still experiencing issues.
Zac Hall is a Senior Editor, covering Apple, apps, and AI.
Downdetector is showing reports across multiple Apple services, even as Apple’s System Status page continues to list them as available.
Check out 9to5Mac on YouTube for more Apple news:
iCloud is built into every Apple device, so that…
AirPods 5 | Apple’s newest wireless headphones
Apple confirms a number of services experiencing issues on its general and developer status pages.
The iPhone maker’s System Status page indicates that there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all users,” which could make the service slow or unavailable.
The App Store, AppleCare on Device, and Apple Music are also experiencing issues, the page indicates.
Like all major tech companies, Apple faces outages and other technical issues affecting its cloud services at times.
This could cause your iPhone to ask for your Apple ID and password, and you could see other attempts to sign in to services with your Apple account information fail.

Apple responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment (which it initially gave to Bloomberg ), noting that the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning.
We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement read.
After a recent slew of tech outages, service disruptions, and flight chaos this week, it’s now Apple customers who are facing technical issues.
Given the recent increase in AI-driven cyberattacks, users across social media have already begun to speculate about the cause.

In particular, users are expressing concerns about the Apple outage, as it arrives only days after technical failures at Microsoft led to its cloud systems that power flagship services like Outlook and Teams failing due to cascading software issues .

extraction.body: An update gone awry at Apple followed a rash of major outages in recent days, among them the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines and Microsoft, highlighting the risks that go along with the massive scope of modern technological platforms. Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages and that its iCloud sign-in interface was designated as also having issues. The technology monitoring site Downdetector.com showed showed a spike in user complaints about Apple Pay as well. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company said in an emailed statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.” Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, was also having technology issues that guests reported had impacted reservations and check-ins, among other problems, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage. Marriott, which has 10,200 properties and more than 1.8 million rooms under its corporate umbrella, has not responded to an email inquiry from The AP. The outages at Marriott and Apple are just the latest in a string of technology breakdowns in recent days. On Monday, a system outage at United Airlines lasted more than 90 minutes, forcing the carrier to delay departing flights. The problem at United came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop that delayed hundreds of flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country. Chicago-based United said there was no indication that its outage was cybersecurity related. Also Monday, thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said Monday that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and as of Tuesday confirmed that the bank's systems were back up and operating normally. Last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. The tech giant said that there was “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

extraction.body: An update gone awry at Apple followed a rash of major outages in recent days, among them the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines and Microsoft, highlighting the risks that go along with the massive scope of modern technological platforms. Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages and that its iCloud sign-in interface was designated as also having issues. The technology monitoring site Downdetector.com showed showed a spike in user complaints about Apple Pay as well. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company said in an emailed statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.” Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, was also having technology issues that guests reported had impacted reservations and check-ins, among other problems, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage. Marriott, which has 10,200 properties and more than 1.8 million rooms under its corporate umbrella, has not responded to an email inquiry from The AP. The outages at Marriott and Apple are just the latest in a string of technology breakdowns in recent days. On Monday, a system outage at United Airlines lasted more than 90 minutes, forcing the carrier to delay departing flights. The problem at United came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop that delayed hundreds of flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country. Chicago-based United said there was no indication that its outage was cybersecurity related. Also Monday, thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said Monday that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and as of Tuesday confirmed that the bank's systems were back up and operating normally. Last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. The tech giant said that there was “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

Apple acknowledged on its system status page that its Apple Music, App Store and AppleCare services suffered full outages and that its iCloud sign-in interface was also having issues. The technology monitoring site Downdetector.com also showed a spike in user complaints about Apple Pay.

“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” the company said in an emailed statement. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”
Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, also had technology issues, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage.

In an emailed statement, Marriott said it has “resolved a technical issue” that affected sign-in capabilities on Marriott.com and the Marriott Bonvoy app. The company added that a company review found no sign the problem “was cybersecurity-related.”
The outages are the latest in a string of technology breakdowns.

On Monday, a system outage at United Airlines lasted more than 90 minutes, forcing the carrier to delay departing flights. The problem at United came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop that delayed hundreds of flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country.
Chicago-based United said there was no indication its outage was cybersecurity-related.

Also Monday, thousands of customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major U.S. banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
Chase said Monday the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and on Tuesday confirmed the bank’s systems were operating normally.

Last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted.

The tech giant said there was “no indication” that malicious activity caused the disruptions, specifically noting on Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

extraction.body: A highly classified communications network used by the National Security Agency went down Tuesday, forcing changes to employee arrival schedules as officials assessed the disruption, CNN reported. The White House said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. The network, known as NSANet, enables employees to exchange classified information internally. Six people familiar with the matter told CNN that the system was down, although the cause, duration, and full extent of the outage remained unclear. The agency implemented staggered arrivals for personnel while working to understand the problem, the sources said. CNN reported that it had requested comment from the NSA. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis sought to reassure Americans that the disruption did not amount to a national security emergency. "We see no evidence that this was a cyberattack," Bis said Tuesday on Newsmax, according to CNN. "There is no crisis, or anything like that, for Americans to be worried about." The failure occurred while President Donald Trump was traveling in Asia, but a current U.S. official and a former official told CNN that the outage would not prevent the delivery of urgent intelligence to the president aboard Air Force One. Both officials described multiple backup networks and redundancies that would allow the government to maintain secure communications with Trump despite the failure of the NSA's internal system. Trump was in the Philippines on Tuesday before a scheduled Wednesday trip to China for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, according to CNN. Although NSANet's failure disrupted an important channel for employees, the officials cited by CNN said alternative systems remained available to transmit sensitive presidential intelligence. Intelligence exchanges with key U.S. allies also remained unaffected, according to a source from a Five Eyes member country and a former U.S. intelligence official who spoke to CNN. The Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance comprises the United States, Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Those sources said the system used to share intelligence among the countries had not been impacted by the NSANet outage. The disruption followed several major technology failures affecting air travel, banking and workplace communications. The reporting did not establish a connection among the incidents or identify a common cause. On Friday, a nationwide ground stop halted flights for hours after a systems failure, resulting in thousands of delays and cancellations. CNN reported that the Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas. A Microsoft outage last week prevented people around the world from accessing Outlook email and Teams meetings. On Monday, thousands of Chase customers reported problems using their online accounts. There was no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages resulted from cyberattacks, according to CNN. The timing of the failures alone does not establish that they were related. passages: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter.
“While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues.
But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security.

extraction.body: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said. The agency reverted to its typical work schedule Tuesday evening. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a three-level system that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The New York Times first reported that detail. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time. This story has been updated with additional information. Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP).

extraction.body: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said. The agency reverted to its typical work schedule Tuesday evening. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a three-level system that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The New York Times first reported that detail. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time. extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. The Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia following last week’s shock resignation of CEO Jensen Huang amid revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, sources told The Post on Tuesday. They said the probe will focus on whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors — likely examining the company’s denial earlier this year that the fallen tech titan was having an affair with Alice Huang, no relation, of Singapore-based Megaspeed. The ex-Nvidia CEO confessed Nov. 8 to an affair with the woman, an alleged Chinese spy, as reports of affairs with two Nvidia employees surfaced. An SEC spokesperson declined to confirm the probe, telling The Post that the agency “does not comment on the existence or nonexistence of a possible investigation.” Huang signaled Tuesday that he would be willing to reclaim the chief executive job if the company’s board asked him. Nvidia’s directors say that’s not on the table, as The Post reported, despite pressure from employees, prominent investors and tech heavyweights like Elon Musk. Nvidia shares jumped nearly 3% in after-hours trading Tuesday after the chipmaking giant reported better-than-expected quarterly earnings, with adjusted profits of $2.68 a share topping Wall Street estimates of $2.48. Revenue of $115.8 billion also beat forecasts of roughly $109 billion, while the company projected fourth-quarter sales of about $130 billion — ahead of analysts’ expectations of $125 billion. Huang said Tuesday he had been overwhelmed by support from Nvidia employees, investors and business partners urging him to return to the company he co-founded. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.” The 63-year-old billionaire made clear that he would welcome a comeback — provided Nvidia’s board agreed to reinstate him. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said. Huang also acknowledged his personal misconduct and pledged to cooperate with an independent investigation commissioned by Nvidia’s directors. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” he said. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” He ended the statement with a personal message to his family. “To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.” Nvidia’s board, however, is not considering reinstating Huang despite growing pressure from prominent investors, employees and Silicon Valley heavyweights, according to reports. Nvidia has named longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent replacement for Huang. President Trump weighed in Monday, saying he would support Huang’s return to the helm of the AI chipmaking giant. Musk has also backed a petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement, joining other prominent tech executives including Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Replit CEO Amjad Masad. At the center of the scandal is Huang’s affair with Alice Huang of Megaspeed International, a technology company that came under federal scrutiny over suspected efforts to divert advanced Nvidia chips to China. US intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang of having ties to China’s Ministry of State Security, according to published reports. Those allegations remain under investigation, and there has been no public finding that Jensen Huang knowingly shared corporate secrets or helped Beijing evade US export restrictions. The scandal deepened when the New York Times reported that Huang had also been romantically involved with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reportedly answered directly to the billionaire CEO. The pair were spotted behaving affectionately during Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose in March, according to the Times. Axios separately reported that Huang’s security team allegedly offered a nondisclosure agreement to a bystander who recorded an interaction between the two. Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a November 8 apology to employees but did not identify either woman. Nvidia subsequently launched an independent investigation into the allegations, retaining former federal prosecutor Joon H. Kim and the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.

They said the probe will focus on whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors — likely examining the company’s denial earlier this year that the fallen tech titan was having an affair with Alice Huang, no relation, of Singapore-based Megaspeed.
The ex-Nvidia CEO confessed Nov. 8 to an affair with the woman, an alleged Chinese spy, as reports of affairs with two Nvidia employees surfaced.
An SEC spokesperson declined to confirm the probe, telling The Post that the agency “does not comment on the existence or nonexistence of a possible investigation.”
Huang signaled Tuesday that he would be willing to reclaim the chief executive job if the company’s board asked him.
Nvidia’s directors say that’s not on the table, as The Post reported, despite pressure from employees, prominent investors and tech heavyweights like Elon Musk.

Nvidia shares jumped nearly 3% in after-hours trading Tuesday after the chipmaking giant reported better-than-expected quarterly earnings, with adjusted profits of $2.68 a share topping Wall Street estimates of $2.48.
Revenue of $115.8 billion also beat forecasts of roughly $109 billion, while the company projected fourth-quarter sales of about $130 billion — ahead of analysts’ expectations of $125 billion.
Huang said Tuesday he had been overwhelmed by support from Nvidia employees, investors and business partners urging him to return to the company he co-founded.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said.
“Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.”
The 63-year-old billionaire made clear that he would welcome a comeback — provided Nvidia’s board agreed to reinstate him.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said.
Huang also acknowledged his personal misconduct and pledged to cooperate with an independent investigation commissioned by Nvidia’s directors.
“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” he said.
“I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.”
He ended the statement with a personal message to his family.
“To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.”
Nvidia’s board, however, is not considering reinstating Huang despite growing pressure from prominent investors, employees and Silicon Valley heavyweights, according to reports.
Nvidia has named longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent replacement for Huang.
President Trump weighed in Monday, saying he would support Huang’s return to the helm of the AI chipmaking giant.
Musk has also backed a petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement, joining other prominent tech executives including Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Replit CEO Amjad Masad.

At the center of the scandal is Huang’s affair with Alice Huang of Megaspeed International, a technology company that came under federal scrutiny over suspected efforts to divert advanced Nvidia chips to China.
US intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang of having ties to China’s Ministry of State Security, according to published reports.
Those allegations remain under investigation, and there has been no public finding that Jensen Huang knowingly shared corporate secrets or helped Beijing evade US export restrictions.

The scandal deepened when the New York Times reported that Huang had also been romantically involved with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reportedly answered directly to the billionaire CEO.
The pair were spotted behaving affectionately during Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose in March, according to the Times.
Axios separately reported that Huang’s security team allegedly offered a nondisclosure agreement to a bystander who recorded an interaction between the two.
Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a November 8 apology to employees but did not identify either woman.
Nvidia subsequently launched an independent investigation into the allegations, retaining former federal prosecutor Joon H. Kim and the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.

A post circulating on X claims Nvidia founder Jensen Huang transferred billions of dollars in company stock to his heirs before resigning as CEO.

Crypto Briefing has not independently confirmed the transfers or the resignation through Nvidia filings or company statements. What follows reflects the X post and the research findings that accompany it.

According to the research findings, Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s president, CEO, and board member on November 12, 2026. The board reportedly accepted his resignation one day earlier, on November 11.
The leadership handoff described in the findings is immediate. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s CFO, would step in as interim CEO. Harvey C. Jones would become the board’s first chair.

Markets reportedly reacted the way markets usually do to surprises at the top. Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% on November 12, according to the findings, wiping out a substantial chunk of market value.
The findings put Huang’s beneficial ownership at approximately 811 to 870 million Nvidia shares. That works out to about 3.4% to 3.58% of the company.
The research values that position at between $130 and $150 billion.
Much of that stake does not sit in Huang’s name directly. About 530 million shares are reportedly held through the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Living Trust.

Another roughly 140 million shares are held in aggregate through irrevocable trusts, according to the findings. A living trust is generally something the founder can still control and change. An irrevocable trust, as the name suggests, is harder to unwind once assets go in. The X post’s claim that shares went to Huang’s heirs fits most naturally with that second bucket, though the findings do not tie specific transfers to specific dates.
The findings say Huang forfeited around $108 million in unvested equity awards when he resigned.
Against a stake reportedly worth $130 to $150 billion, $108 million is a rounding error. Walking away from it suggests the exit was not a leisurely, planned retirement on a vesting schedule.

The research findings flag a potential investigation into the circumstances of Huang’s departure. They also warn that such a probe could cause lasting reputational damage to Nvidia and weigh on investor confidence.

None of the material reviewed alleges that the share transfers broke any rule. Moving stock to heirs is not the same as selling it. A transfer into a family trust does not put cash in anyone’s pocket or dump shares onto the market.
The research notes that the leadership change may introduce volatility, with investors uncertain about strategic direction under an interim chief.
The second issue is ownership overhang. A founder controlling roughly 3.4% to 3.58% of the company, now outside the building, is a stake the market will watch closely.
The third issue is governance. Appointing Harvey C. Jones as the board’s first chair signals a formal separation of oversight from management.

What to watch next: Nvidia’s own regulatory filings detailing the trust transfers and their dates, any statement on the reported investigation, and whether the board moves quickly to name a permanent CEO. The 4.3% drop was the first verdict. The filings will be the evidence.

extraction.body: Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday was its first with CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress at the helm alongside the company’s first board chair, Harvey C. The leadership change followed Jensen Huang’s resignation last week after reports he had multiple affairs – including one with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang and one with a direct report, Kimberly Powell. Nvidia is investigating whether Huang’s relationship with the former compromised national security or company secrets. Huang will also testify before lawmakers on December 1st. Ahead of Tuesday’s earnings, Huang said he would be willing to return as CEO. However, during the company’s earnings call, Jones stated that “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted [Huang’s] resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones also said that during the call, the company would not be addressing or taking questions “regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.” He added that, “the Board is proactively dealing with the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward.” In Tuesday’s earnings Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, continuing years of skyrocketing revenue driven by the AI industry. Jones shared the following update on the company: > As Chairman of NVIDIA’s Board of Directors, I want to say a few words on the Board’s behalf. Our financial performance speaks for itself. > On November 12th, our Board of Directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as President, CEO, and board member. The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO. The Board appointed Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s longtime and well-respected CFO, as interim CEO. In addition, the Board announced it was initiating a search for a permanent chief executive, and we have since retained Heidrick and Struggles to lead the search. > While this was an unexpected transition, the Board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company’s employees, customers, partners, and shareholders. This morning, the company announced that our Board has established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee that will include a select group of our independent Board directors, senior external advisors, and legal counsel. > This committee will enhance— will– excuse me, will enhance our engagement with the U.S. government, including all relevant agencies. We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation. Our Board will communicate further when appropriate. On behalf of our shareholders, the Board is proactively dealing with the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward. > We have an incredibly talented leadership team, and we have every confidence in Colette’s leadership, integrity, and ability to deliver as interim CEO. Colette has been at the center of this company’s extraordinary growth for the last— growth for the last 13 years, instrumental in executing strategy, and with a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations, and financial position. The Board and the entire leadership team remain laser-focused on driving NVIDIA forward. Kress responded to a question about the company’s leadership transition, saying “the most important thing that we think through right now is our employees.” She added, “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual.” Jones also gave an update on Nvidia’s search for a new permanent CEO: > From the board’s point of view, we take the search very seriously. The Board appreciates that we’re living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace. Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So, the search will be thorough and we want to install the CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.

coreStoryFacts.text: Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday was its first with CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress at the helm alongside the company’s first board chair, Harvey C.

The leadership change followed Jensen Huang’s resignation last week after reports he had multiple affairs – including one with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang and one with a direct report, Kimberly Powell.
Nvidia is investigating whether Huang’s relationship with the former compromised national security or company secrets.
The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.
The Board and the entire leadership team remain laser-focused on driving NVIDIA forward.

Our earlier coverage is below.Nvidia's board of directors is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang soon, according to two sources familiar with the matter, following allegations that Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believe was a Chinese asset.The Trump administration is aware of the matter, the sources said.The Wall Street Journal was first to report on the board's moves.

Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws."China has denied all allegations, with Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun telling reporters on Monday that the "so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear."Beyond the national security concerns, Nvidia is facing a securities lawsuit accusing the company of failing to disclose information to shareholders about Jensen Huang's relationship with the alleged spy.

The company has faced days of turmoil following reports that American intelligence agencies believed Huang was the target of a Chinese spying plot.Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993, and for years it was best known for designing graphics cards widely used for gaming.
President Trump gave Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 computer chips to "approved customers" in China late last year, with the federal government taking a 25% cut of chip sales.
The deal did not include Nvidia's more advanced Blackwell or Rubin systems.

Trump called Jensen Huang a "very high-quality person," saying during a White House briefing that "the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape." The president said he spoke to Jensen Huang to see how he was doing, and the executive "said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."
Both are married to other people.Huang, Powell and Nvidia have not commented on the Times report.
Nvidia is opening an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort," the company's board of directors said Sunday.
"I love our country and our company," Jensen Huang said.
"I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security."
In a letter to Nvidia employees obtained by The Associated Press, Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologized to his family and colleagues.
He said he took "full responsibility" for his actions.

Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia.
Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times.
Nvidia's board said it has "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.
Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it," the board said.
"Today's news will not slow Nvidia," company spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement.
"Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption."
Asked whether he wished he had acted on intelligence when he was briefed about spying, Trump again praised Huang: "I think he's an honorable guy.

extraction.body: Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday was its first with CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress at the helm alongside the company’s first board chair, Harvey C. The leadership change followed Jensen Huang’s resignation last week after reports he had multiple affairs – including one with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang and one with a direct report, Kimberly Powell. Nvidia is investigating whether Huang’s relationship with the former compromised national security or company secrets. Huang will also testify before lawmakers on December 1st. Ahead of Tuesday’s earnings, Huang said he would be willing to return as CEO. However, during the company’s earnings call, Jones stated that “the Nvidia board unanimously accepted [Huang’s] resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Jones also said that during the call, the company would not be addressing or taking questions “regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation.” He added that, “the Board is proactively dealing with the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward.” In Tuesday’s earnings Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, continuing years of skyrocketing revenue driven by the AI industry. Jones shared the following update on the company: > As Chairman of NVIDIA’s Board of Directors, I want to say a few words on the Board’s behalf. Our financial performance speaks for itself. > On November 12th, our Board of Directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as President, CEO, and board member. The NVIDIA Board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO. The Board appointed Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s longtime and well-respected CFO, as interim CEO. In addition, the Board announced it was initiating a search for a permanent chief executive, and we have since retained Heidrick and Struggles to lead the search. > While this was an unexpected transition, the Board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company’s employees, customers, partners, and shareholders. This morning, the company announced that our Board has established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee that will include a select group of our independent Board directors, senior external advisors, and legal counsel. > This committee will enhance— will– excuse me, will enhance our engagement with the U.S. government, including all relevant agencies. We will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation. Our Board will communicate further when appropriate. On behalf of our shareholders, the Board is proactively dealing with the immediate consequences facing the company, as well as enhancing our oversight capacity going forward. > We have an incredibly talented leadership team, and we have every confidence in Colette’s leadership, integrity, and ability to deliver as interim CEO. Colette has been at the center of this company’s extraordinary growth for the last— growth for the last 13 years, instrumental in executing strategy, and with a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations, and financial position. The Board and the entire leadership team remain laser-focused on driving NVIDIA forward. Kress responded to a question about the company’s leadership transition, saying “the most important thing that we think through right now is our employees.” She added, “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual.” Jones also gave an update on Nvidia’s search for a new permanent CEO: > From the board’s point of view, we take the search very seriously. The Board appreciates that we’re living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace. Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So, the search will be thorough and we want to install the CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.

extraction.body: A pedestrian walks in front of a Nvidia sign outside the company's headquarters on Nov. 12, 2026 in Santa Clara, Calif. after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images hide caption Nvidia said it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang, amid a push by the former CEO's allies to return him to lead the chipmaker he cofounded. Huang "voluntarily resigned" on Nov. 12 after disclosing "personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms," board chair Harvey Jones said on the company's earnings call on Tuesday afternoon. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Earlier on Tuesday, Huang had said he would return to lead the company he cofounded if Nvidia's board allowed him to. Huang also agreed to appear before Congress to answer questions about the national security scandals swirling around the company. "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang wrote in a statement posted on social media . "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation." Huang stepped down from the company last week after acknowledging that he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency , as well as with another woman who is an executive at Nvidia. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports. Huang said he would be "honored" to return to the company if Nvidia's board agreed. His comments came as some in Silicon Valley have tried to argue that Huang was pushed out of the company too quickly, and circulated a petition to "stand with Jensen." "We don't want rushes to judgment. We don't want political pressure from the left or the right to force a board into action before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done," said Brad Gerstner, the founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, an investor in Nvidia, at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday. Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will answer questions behind closed doors from the House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committees and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1st and 2nd. Lawmakers say they want answers about Nvidia's role in alleged chip smuggling and efforts to evade export controls meant to block China from accessing the most advanced U.S. AI chips. They will also ask Huang about his involvement with Alice Huang , who was an executive with Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company that was a major customer for Nvidia's chips. In a statement emailed to NPR, Megaspeed said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business," and that Alice Huang left the company in 2025, but that it is conducting an internal investigation. Nvidia's board said on Tuesday it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies, compliance with U.S. export controls, and risk management of global trade. On Monday, the U.S. Commerce Department announced new rules to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that may have let Chinese companies remotely access advanced Nvidia chips through overseas data centers. The Commerce Department and Justice Department also announced Monday that the DOJ is conducting a criminal investigation of Megaspeed. Nvidia sought to reassure investors about the company's future during its third-quarter earnings call on Tuesday. "Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. And our commitment to customers, partners and shareholders will not change," said Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer who is serving as interim CEO while the board finds a permanent leader. Quarterly sales doubled to a record $115.8 billion and profit also doubled to $65.3 billion from a year ago. The company said it was raising its forecast for sales growth next year. Nvidia shares were up 5% in after-hours trading on Tuesday. The company's stock price has dropped more than 16% since Huang admitting having an extramarital affair earlier this month. extraction.body: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said. The agency reverted to its typical work schedule Tuesday evening. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a three-level system that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The New York Times first reported that detail. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time. extraction.body: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said. The agency reverted to its typical work schedule Tuesday evening. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a three-level system that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The New York Times first reported that detail. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time. This story has been updated with additional information. Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP).

extraction.body: (CNN) — The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The network, called NSA Net, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said. CNN has asked the National Security Agency for comment. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSA Net would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Teams meetings. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros. Discovery Company. passages: By Natasha Bertrand, Katie Bo Lillis, Sean Lyngaas, Davis Winkie, Zachary Cohen, CNN
(CNN) — The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter.
The network, called NSA Net, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said.
As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said.
CNN has asked the National Security Agency for comment.
